research_focus: Interpreting morphometric indicators (slope, slope exposition, relief energy, altitude) and their correlations to perform indirect mapping of soil types in the Anieş Hydrographic Basin.
method: GIS raster and vector database integrated in spatial analysis modules were used to analyze morphometric parameters (slope, slope exposition, relief energy) correlated with altitude for indirect mapping of soil types.
application_domain: Soil science and geomorphology: indirect mapping of soil types based on relief morphometric characteristics in a mountainous hydrographic basin.
results_summary: The paper applied morphometric analysis (slope, slope exposition, relief energy) correlated with altitude via GIS-based indirect mapping to identify soil types in the Anieş basin. It identified zone soils (Luvisols, Eutric cambosols, distric cambosols, podzols, prepodzols, criptopodzols, humosiosols) and intra-zone soils (rendzins, lithosols, hystosols, fluvisols). Two characteristic slope intervals were outlined: over 12° at high altitudes and 0–12° along streams and high mountain plateaus. Southern and Eastern expositions were found to dominate the basin, with implications for pedogenetic processes, water retention, and land-use suitability. The study concluded that morphometric factors are essential characters of soil cover that influence pedogenesis, drainage, and soil functionality.
research_gaps: Further studies concerning land usefulness are needed, including correcting soil acidity; Monitoring of lands affected by soil erosion is identified as a necessary follow-up

research_focus: The spatial data handling procedures used to convert historical Coastal Survey Maps (T-sheets) of the Connecticut shoreline into a digital vector database for use in GIS-based coastal resource management.
method: Scanning of paper T-sheets into digital raster images, followed by georectification and vectorization using Geographic Transformer Software 5 and ArcGIS 8.3 to compile a digital line database of the Connecticut shoreline.
application_domain: Coastal geography and shoreline mapping; conversion of historical cartographic documents into digital geospatial databases for monitoring coastal changes over time.
results_summary: The paper documents the step-by-step procedures for converting scanned historical Coastal Survey Maps into a vector database depicting the Connecticut shoreline. The project was carried out as a joint effort between the Connecticut Department of Environmental Protection and the University of Connecticut Center for Geographic Information and Analysis. The resulting vector database can be integrated into modern GIS systems to monitor changes in coastal shorelines over time. The authors emphasize that proper metadata is essential for correct georectification and merging of the historical data into a digital geo-database. Detailed implementation information is provided in an appendix covering the use of Geographic Transformer Software 5 and ArcGIS 8.3.
limitations: The process requires care and sufficient metadata information to ensure the historical data can be correctly geo-rectified and merged into a digital geo-database.

research_focus: Development of a consolidated, reproducible multi-scale methodology to semi-automatically map grey (built-up) and green (vegetation) structures in urban and suburban areas by combining Pléiades satellite imagery with existing geographic vector data.
method: Object-based image analysis (OBIA) on Pléiades satellite images at local scale (1/10,000), combined with existing vector databases (OSM, BDTOPO) as ancillary data, and classification using Random Forest, SVM, and KNN algorithms.
application_domain: Urban land-use/land-cover mapping, urban planning, and biodiversity monitoring in European cities
results_summary: The paper proposes a multi-scale methodology that integrates Pléiades imagery with vector databases (OSM, BDTOPO) to semi-automatically classify grey and green urban structures. Object-based classification was performed using three algorithms (RF, SVM, KNN) on two French cities, Strasbourg and Rennes. Kappa values were satisfactory (all >0.7), with SVM achieving the best result for Strasbourg (Kappa 0.8) and RF for Rennes (Kappa 0.79). RF and SVM demonstrated greater robustness in discriminating difficult classes such as shadows and water. The methodology showed preliminary good results and was also tested on Brussels with similar outcomes.
limitations: Shadow discrimination requires more specific methods; all three classification algorithms show the same limits in correctly extracting shadows; The spatial analysis of urban fabric needs to be completed with additional indexes and evaluated on a greater number of urban fabrics
research_gaps: A consolidated and reproducible methodological framework for mapping European cities using remote sensing data is still missing; The methodology must be evaluated on a large number of urban fabrics to validate its generalizability; The approach needs to be adapted (features selection and composition) for cities characterized by different morphological development patterns

research_focus: Addressing the feature dimensionality reduction problem in Content Based Medical Image Retrieval (CBMIR) systems, which increases computational complexity and decreases retrieval speed, by proposing a hybrid framework combining feature extraction, optimization, classification, and similarity measurement.
method: The proposed FOCS (Feature Optimized Classification Similarity) framework uses GLCM and Tamura Features for texture extraction into a feature vector database, Fuzzy-based Particle Swarm Optimization (FPSO) for dimensionality reduction, Fuzzy-based Relevance Vector Machine (FRVM) for feature classification, and Euclidean Distance for similarity measurement between query and target images.
application_domain: Medical image retrieval for clinical diagnosis and educational research, covering gray-level images of lung, liver, kidney, and brain.
results_summary: The FOCS framework was evaluated on a database of 1000 gray-level medical images covering lung, liver, kidney, and brain. Feature extraction using GLCM and Tamura Features achieved approximately 90% performance, and the optimization and classification phases also reached about 90% performance. In a retrieval performance comparison using 54 testing samples of lung images, the proposed Fuzzy PSO-RVM method demonstrated higher precision and recall than PSO-SVM and PSO-RVM baselines while converging faster in terms of iterations. The authors conclude that the FOCS framework outperforms existing CBMIR systems in retrieval accuracy and precision, reducing computational complexity while increasing response speed.

research_focus: Automatically detecting discrepancies between an existing cartographic vector database (GIS map) and a more recent remote sensing image to support map updating, specifically applied to forest change detection (clear cuts, regeneration, composite objects).
method: An automated workflow combining geographic object-based image analysis (to automatically label image segments using information extracted from the existing vector database) with non-parametric statistical iterative trimming (to detect discrepancies as outliers based on a likelihood threshold α). Median filtering was applied before multi-resolution segmentation to improve class separability.
application_domain: Cartographic vector database updating for forest management (clear cut detection, forest regeneration, land-use/land-cover change detection)
results_summary: The paper designed an automated image-to-map discrepancy detection workflow that requires no interactive training sample selection. Applied to forest map updating, the workflow detected approximately 75% of forest regeneration and 100% of clear cuts with less than 10% commission errors. Detection efficiency was higher for deciduous stands (E = 97.8) than for coniferous stands (E = 92.0). The non-parametric iterative trimming proved flexible across land-cover types, though its sensitivity parameter α must be tuned per application. The method is limited by construction to detecting relatively small proportions (10–20%) of discrepancies between the image and the map.
limitations: The method is limited by construction to relatively small percentages (10 to 20 percent) of discrepancies between the remote sensing data and the map; The segmentation algorithm is a bottleneck because composite objects mislead edge delineation or embed small changed areas inside forest stands; Red and NIR wavelengths were not appropriate for detecting deciduous forest within coniferous objects due to similar reflectance values; The optimal α value varies for different land-cover classes and applications, requiring user tuning; Small objects such as buildings or linear elements were not properly detected due to inappropriate spatial resolution; A crisp classification of discrepancies does not correspond to field complexity, as there is a gradual change between clear cut and mature forest stands; Results cannot be extrapolated from this single case study
research_gaps: Further work is necessary to classify the discrepancy type using existing classification algorithms trained by automatically selected samples; Decision rules have to be developed to assimilate the change information into the vector database; An optimized workflow for other land-cover types should include a step for selecting the most meaningful characteristics (e.g., texture, shape) to discriminate each class; Context and relevant minimum mapping unit information would be necessary to properly process partially changed composite objects

research_focus: Compilation of a comprehensive georeferenced database of Anopheles mosquito vectors in Nigeria, spanning 100 years of published research (1900–2010), to provide a baseline for malaria and lymphatic filariasis vector control programmes.
method: All published data on Anopheles vectors in Nigeria were collated from 110 publications into a single database, recording locality, latitude/longitude, time/period of study, species, abundance, sampling/collection methods, morphological and molecular species identification methods, insecticide resistance status (including kdr allele evidence), P. falciparum sporozoite rate, and W. bancrofti microfilaria prevalence.
application_domain: Vector-borne disease control (malaria and lymphatic filariasis), mosquito vector ecology and epidemiology in Nigeria
results_summary: The authors collated 110 publications covering 484,747 Anopheles mosquitoes at 142 georeferenced locations across Nigeria from 1900 to 2010. The most abundant vectors were the An. gambiae complex (65.2%), An. funestus complex (17.3%), and An. gambiae s.s. (6.5%), with molecular forms M and S identified at 120 locations. Insecticide resistance to pyrethroids and organochlorines was widespread across 45 locations, particularly in the southwestern region. The database revealed a geographical shift in research focus from the northern region in the 20th century to the southern region in recent decades, and highlighted critical gaps in data on An. funestus, species interactions, and systematic same-site sampling over time.
limitations: Total number of mosquitoes collected is underrepresented because numbers were not available in some studies; Species abundance was not specified in some studies, limiting compositional analysis; Very few studies were carried out in the same locations in different years or seasons, restricting analysis of changes over time; Large gaps in data coverage in the eastern regions of Nigeria due to limited accessibility and infrastructure; Very little data from the northwestern region, especially the area of the Garki Project (1960s–70s); Most missing data came from earlier studies (1900–1963) when few species identification options existed; Few studies focused on malaria and LF parasites, making cross-study comparisons difficult; Only one study reported co-infection of Plasmodium parasites and LF in mosquitoes
research_gaps: Research on the composition and distribution of the An. funestus group is needed as it is an important vector for both LF and malaria; The role of An. gambiae M and S molecular forms in malaria and/or LF transmission and how they interact is largely unknown; Simpler and more standardized sampling and collection methods are needed; Consensus standardization of the number and location of surveillance sites and the frequency of insecticide resistance monitoring is required; Widespread systematic sampling across the country is needed for malaria and LF parasite prevalence; Better linkages and partnerships between entomologists, parasitologists, national control programmes, international donors, and other stakeholders are needed; New techniques for egg laying and colonising An. funestus are being developed to facilitate future research opportunities; Same-site collections over time are needed to allow comparisons within and between populations

research_focus: Evaluation of the efficacy of archived NOAA/AVHRR remotely sensed data for creating historic wildfire maps in California, USA, by comparing a remote sensing-based fire map with a state-maintained vector database of fire perimeters across land cover types and ecoregions.
method: Fires from 1996 and 1999 were mapped using NOAA AVHRR sensor data. A vector database of fire perimeters compiled by the State of California was used as a comparison source. The two datasets were overlaid and spatially compared across land cover types and ten ecoregions, with sources of disagreement and overlap quantified to assess fire detection algorithm performance.
application_domain: Wildfire mapping and burn scar detection using remote sensing, with spatial comparison across land cover types and ecoregions in California
results_summary: The study compared AVHRR-based wildfire maps for 1996 and 1999 against a California state vector database of fire perimeters, quantifying overlap and disagreement across land cover types and ecoregions. Results showed that algorithm performance varies significantly over land cover types, with forest lands being mapped more effectively than any other cover type. The percent mapping accuracy was similar across the two fire years, reinforcing the conclusion that the algorithm is most effective for forest lands. Different NDVI change thresholds and time intervals resulted in only approximately 10% difference in mapping success between 1996 and 1999, and the relative accuracy across cover types was only slightly affected by these parameter differences.
limitations: Algorithm performance for burn scar detection is significantly lower for non-forest land cover types compared to forest lands; AVHRR data were the only available data source before 2000 and were subsequently replaced by other data sets such as MODIS, limiting the temporal scope of the analysis

research_focus: The alignment and harmonization of geospatial vector databases that cover similar spatial extent but exhibit geometric discrepancies due to differences in accuracy, scale, data collection methods, and level-of-detail.
method: A localized geometric alignment process that exploits local spatial, topologic, and geometric relationships between corresponding line-features, quantifies local distortions via specifically selected observation constraints, and applies Least Squares Adjustment (LSA) to achieve spatial consistency.
application_domain: Geospatial data alignment, specifically cadastral and topographic vector databases containing line-features (borders, roads) and polygon features.
results_summary: The proposed localized geometric alignment approach was demonstrated on three examples. In the first, geometric discrepancies such as gaps and continuity issues between vector databases were reduced to zero after alignment. In the second, alignment of a cadastral database with a topographic reference database reduced residuals from 17.98/84.36 m² to 0.42/1.12 m² over three iterations, achieving complete feature overlay. In the third, a synthetic affine transformation was recovered with calculated parameters very close to the original values, with standard deviations of approximately +/-0.1 m in translation parameters. The results confirm that the local adjustment strategy resolves geometric distortions that global affine transformations cannot address.
limitations: The alignment model has a local fashion, which introduces small standard deviations in the calculated transformation parameters; The adjustment equations identify point-to-line correspondences rather than point-to-point correspondences; In some cases, mere geometric analysis of possible corresponding features is not successful because several neighboring objects are possible candidates
research_gaps: Adding more constraints to handle poor geometry constellation of data, such as sparsely distributed points and excessive points; Analyzing larger databases with wider coverage areas, which will increase the size of the normal equation system to be solved; Applying hierarchical partitioning of space (e.g., using the major road network as high-level objects) to reduce the number of features involved in the adjustment; Incorporating supplementary data such as semantics, attributes, and other topological characteristics to better identify corresponding features when geometric analysis alone is insufficient

research_focus: Automatic detection of building changes (new, demolished, and planimetrically inaccurate) between a vector cartographic database and more recent satellite imagery and lidar data, to support semi-automatic updating of 1:25,000 scale topographic maps.
method: Support vector machine (SVM) classification applied to a joint SPOT5 multispectral satellite image and lidar (DSM/DTM) dataset, with SVM training automatically derived from the existing vector geospatial database. Results are visualized using a traffic-light map to assist human operators in final cartographic editing.
application_domain: Cartography and geospatial database updating, specifically building change detection for topographic map revision
results_summary: The paper proposes an SVM-based semi-automatic method that detects new buildings, demolished buildings, and planimetric inaccuracies by comparing a vector cartographic database with SPOT5 satellite imagery and lidar data. The method achieved 98% accuracy in detecting building changes, validated through numerical evaluation and ROC curves. SPOT5 imagery with two infrared bands proved more effective than higher-resolution PNOA aerial imagery for discriminating buildings from vegetation, despite the latter's superior spatial resolution. Small buildings surrounded by tall vegetation and structures with atypical spectral signatures (e.g., a purple tile roof) remained challenging, producing false negatives. The tiling-based implementation allows the method to scale to any data size, making it suitable for industrial cartographic production.
limitations: Small houses and low buildings surrounded by high trees present significant problems for automatic detection; SPOT5 resolution of 2.5 m limits detection to buildings with a ground footprint larger than 2.5 m × 2.5 m; Errors in the DTM derived from the lidar DSM (e.g., steep-sided hills mistaken for buildings) propagate into the final change map; Buildings with unusual spectral signatures, such as a purple tile roof, can be missed as false negatives; Bridges on highways are falsely detected as buildings because they appear with height in the DSM; Noise in the classification results requires additional processing (e.g., mathematical morphology opening) for cleanup; Incoherencies in the vector cartography coding (e.g., code 11 assigned instead of code 41) produce spurious change detections
research_gaps: Future acquisition of aerial images in RGB plus near-infrared bands could improve detection of smaller buildings currently undetectable with SPOT5; The method would need small modifications to be applicable to new RGB + NIR aerial data planned by the Spanish NMA; Comparison with other methods in the literature is difficult because existing approaches use different input data, classification algorithms, and amounts of manual work

research_focus: Developing an efficient and effective content-based image retrieval (CBIR) system that extracts color, texture, and shape features of color images using a unified framework based on the Full Range Autoregressive (FRAR) model with Bayesian approach, combined with RBFNN-based categorization and short-term learning relevance feedback to reduce the semantic gap.
method: A common framework based on the FRAR model with Bayesian approach is used to extract color autocorrelogram, improved edge histogram descriptor (EHD), and micro-texture (MT) features from color images in HSV color space. application_domain: Content-based image retrieval (CBIR) for color images, with stated applications in medicine, engineering, education, and research
results_summary: The paper proposes a unified FRAR model with Bayesian approach framework to extract color autocorrelogram, improved EHD, and micro-texture features from color images in HSV color space. The system demonstrates robustness against illumination changes, viewing angle variations, scaling, and rotation. The computational complexity of the proposed technique is lower than that of MPEG-7 based descriptor combinations and JCD. The results indicate that the proposed system maintains a balance between feature vector dimensions, retrieval performance, and computational cost.
research_gaps: Incorporation of other machine learning mechanisms for further improvement of the proposed system

research_focus: Identification and mapping of paleochannels to reconstruct the migration of the Serchio River in the Lucca alluvial plain (Tuscany, Italy) using a multidisciplinary GIS-based approach combining remote sensing and stratigraphic data.
method: Processing remote sensing imagery of different resolutions (aerial orthophotos at 1 m and 50 cm, satellite images at 15 m) to enhance buried fluvial features, then comparing detected features with stratigraphic investigations (penetration tests, boreholes), archaeological surveys, geomorphological maps, and previous remote sensing studies. All identified traces were mapped and compiled in a georeferenced interactive vector database within a GIS environment.
application_domain: Geospatial data and geomorphology: mapping paleoriver migration and paleochannels in alluvial plains
results_summary: The paper applied a multidisciplinary GIS-based approach combining multi-resolution remote sensing imagery with stratigraphic, archaeological, and geomorphological data to identify paleochannels in the Lucca alluvial plain. Two main paleochannel systems were identified: a primary system (channels >2.5 km long, 50–300 m wide) and a secondary system (channels <1.5 km long, <20 m wide). A total of 169 fluvial elements were mapped and stored in a georeferenced vector database with attributes including type, hierarchy, identification degree, and length. The results confirmed major features from previous studies and, thanks to higher-resolution aerial photos, enabled the discovery of smaller secondary channels. The secondary traces suggest a drainage network possibly linked to Roman-era land reclamation and channelling for agriculture.
limitations: Comparison with previous studies was difficult because the size of investigated fluvial elements is highly variable and a secondary system was often not distinguished in earlier works; Imperfect spatial match with previous studies is attributed to the different spatial resolution of the analyzed images

research_focus: Building a comprehensive, integrated multi-scale spatial database for Emergency Management in India, with standards for integrating heterogeneous geospatial data (vector, raster, non-spatial) and disseminating it through web services for effective emergency response.
method: Defining standards and procedures for data integration (standard coding scheme, schema, metadata format, spatial format), database organization (data management, catalogues, data models), and database dissemination through web services, applied to the National Database for Emergency Management (NDEM) in India.

research_focus: Improving content-based image retrieval (CBIR) efficiency by applying histogram modification functions (EQH, LOG, POLY, Linear Equations) to reduce feature vector dimensionality to 64 bins using center of gravity partitioning of R, G, B color histograms.
method: Color histograms are modified using four functions (EQH, POLY, LOG, LinearEQ1/2/3), partitioned into 64 bins via center of gravity, statistical moments (mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis) are computed per bin for each color channel, and retrieval is evaluated using three similarity measures (Euclidean distance, absolute distance, cosine correlation distance) with PRCP, LS, and LSRR performance metrics on a 2000-image database.
application_domain: Content-based image retrieval (CBIR)
results_summary: The paper evaluated four histogram modification functions combined with a 64-bin center-of-gravity partitioning approach on a database of 2000 images across 20 categories. LOG and POLY functions were found to perform best overall, with LOG being superior in 6 out of 12 comparison cases across moments and similarity measures. The PRCP values crossed 0.5, indicating improved retrieval performance over both the original histogram and the commonly used equalized histogram baseline. Among similarity measures, absolute distance (AD) showed the lowest computational complexity, while cosine correlation and Euclidean distance performed well in cases where AD failed. LS values reached up to 75 and LSRR values were around 10-15%, demonstrating the system's potential for efficient and relevant image retrieval.

research_focus: The paper explores a histogram bins matching approach for Content Based Image Retrieval (CBIR), specifically investigating the effect of dimensionality reduction by linearly grouping histogram bins from 256 to 32 and 16 on retrieval performance.

research_focus: Proposing and testing a method for change detection of polygonal data in the spatial vector database ZB GIS® using object-based image analysis, without requiring classification of image segments, while leveraging data already contained in the database for both segmentation and change detection.
method: Two levels of image segmentation are performed (first according to input vector data, second based on vector and spectral data), followed by rule-based reclassification of second-level segments to identify changes. application_domain: Spatial vector database update, remote sensing image analysis, land cover change detection, geographic information systems
results_summary: The proposed object-based change detection method achieved overall classification accuracies of 87.12% in the Malženice agricultural landscape and 84.55% in the Chopok-jasná mountainous landscape. research_focus: Large-scale approximate nearest neighbor search for unstructured high-dimensional vectors, specifically addressing the limited performance of product quantization on such data.
method: Residual vector quantization is used to encode database vectors into short codes composed of quantization indices. Two search approaches are proposed: an exhaustive search based on fast asymmetric distance computation, and a non-exhaustive search method for large-scale scenarios.
indexing_methods: KD-tree; hierarchical k-means (HKM); E2LSH; spectral hashing; product quantization; hamming embedding; miniBOF; small hashing code; small binary code; residual vector quantization
application_domain: Computer vision applications including keypoint matching, object retrieval, image classification, and scene recognition
results_summary: The paper introduces residual vector quantization as an encoding method for approximate nearest neighbor search, targeting the known weakness of product quantization on unstructured vector data. Two search approaches are proposed: an exhaustive search based on fast asymmetric distance computation and a non-exhaustive search for large-scale scenarios. The approaches are evaluated on two structured and one unstructured dataset, compared against spectral hashing and product quantization. Results show that the proposed methods achieve the best trade-off between search quality, speed, and memory usage. On unstructured data the approaches significantly outperform product quantization, while on structured data they slightly outperform it.

research_focus: Improving Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) performance by proposing a novel feature extraction approach that modifies image histograms using polynomial functions to shift them toward lower intensities, then partitions the modified histograms into 8 bins using center of gravity to form a compact feature vector.
method: Images are separated into R, G, B planes; histograms are computed and modified using three polynomial functions (y=x², y=x³, y=x⁴); modified histograms are partitioned into two parts using center of gravity to form 8 bins; features (pixel count, total of intensities, average of intensities) are extracted per bin; 21 feature vector databases are generated; retrieval is performed using Euclidean distance, Absolute distance, and Cosine correlation distance; performance is evaluated using PRCP, Longest String, and LSRR metrics on a database of 2000 BMP images from 20 classes with 200 query images.
application_domain: Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) / image search
results_summary: The paper tested 21 feature vector databases generated from three polynomial functions and three bin-content types (count, total, average of intensities) using 2000 BMP images across 20 classes and 200 query images. The polynomial y=x² consistently outperformed y=x³ and y=x⁴ across most evaluation metrics (PRCP, Longest String, LSRR). After combining R, G, and B color results using an OR criterion, the best PRCP reached 0.45, which the authors consider a good achievement for a CBIR system. The 8-bin feature vector significantly reduced computational complexity compared to traditional 256-bin histogram approaches. The green color channel generally yielded the best results, and average LSRR values ranged between 60% and 70% traversal of the database.

research_focus: Estimation of soil water retention capacity (WRC) using pedotransfer functions (PTF) compatible with a vector database of classified soil-ecological units in the Slovak Republic, and mapping the spatial distribution of the cumulative coefficient of water retention capacity (CWRC) in the case-study areas of Levoča and Hriňová.
method: The authors developed a model algorithm from selected parameters (particle size, bulk density, organic carbon, morphometric parameters) compatible with the vector database of classified soil-ecological units, using pedotransfer functions (multiple linear regression models) to indirectly estimate hydrolimits. The algorithm was applied to two cadastre areas (Levoča and Hriňová) to categorize and map WRC.
mentioned_systems: vector database of classified soil-ecological units (Slovak Republic); HYPRES (Hydraulic Properties of European Soils); 1:1,000,000 Soil Geographical Database of Eurasia; 1:1,000,000 Soil Database of Europe
application_domain: Soil hydrology, land-use planning, and flood-risk assessment in agricultural landscapes of the Slovak Republic
results_summary: The authors created a model algorithm compatible with the vector database of classified soil-ecological units to estimate and spatially distribute the cumulative coefficient of water retention capacity (CWRC). In the Levoča case study, 18% of agricultural land fell in the medium RWC category, compared to only 5.6% in Hriňová, while both areas showed a high share (31–50%) of very low to low RWC soils, largely determined by local geomorphology. Soils with medium and higher retention capacity were mainly loamy fluvisols in floodplains and, in Hriňová, cambisols on volcanic substrates. The results enable identification of flood-risk areas and support land-use and landscape management decisions for sustainable water-resource protection.
limitations: Existing pedotransfer functions are deficient for the complex evaluation of soil cover due to disagreements about attributes; The listed PTFs cannot be directly used for the vector database of classified soil-ecological units; Direct measurement of soil hydrological data is very difficult in terms of capacity; Possibilities to compare simulations with field measurements are limited, requiring careful interpretation of results

research_focus: The paper investigates how the relationship between sky view factor (SVF) and land surface temperature (LST) as indicators of urban morphology's impact on the urban heat island effect depends on spatial resolution, ranging from coarse satellite to very fine airborne scales.
method: Multiple daytime thermal images from Landsat 8 TIRS, ASTER, and airborne TASI-600 sensors acquired in different months were used to retrieve LST. A three-dimensional building vector database was used to produce SVF maps at matching spatial resolutions. Correlation analyses and weighted linear regressions were performed to assess the SVF-LST relationship across scales.
application_domain: Urban heat island assessment and urban morphology analysis using multi-resolution remote sensing (satellite and airborne thermal imagery) and 3D building data
results_summary: A positive relationship between daytime LST and SVF was confirmed for all three sensor types, consistent with existing literature. For same-sensor images, the SVF-LST trends are almost superimposable with only minor variations in regression coefficients. However, significant differences emerge when comparing data from different sensors/resolutions, attributed to micro-scale factors (thermal properties of building materials, anthropogenic heat, humidity, pollutants) that are smoothed out at macro-scale. The analysis indicates a minimum resolution element of 30 m for the study case, and that the optimal spatial resolution cannot be univocally determined but must be tuned to the specific application scale (micro-scale urban districts vs. macro-scale UHI analysis).
limitations: The lack of reliable cartographic digital data can be a limiting factor when airborne thermal data are used; The dataset used for SVF computation must be consistent with the resolution of airborne thermal data, which is not always available; It is difficult to identify a reference sample to set the spatial resolution scale; The optimal spatial resolution cannot be univocally determined
research_gaps: Studies on how spatial resolution affects the LST-SVF relationship were missing in the literature prior to this work; The choice of spatial resolution should be tuned based on the specific application, implying the need for further guidance on scale selection for different urban analysis purposes

research_focus: Designing and implementing a real-time updating system for the Turkish Topographic Vector Database (TOPOVT) that enables governmental institutions and municipalities to contribute geospatial data updates via the internet, thereby avoiding duplicate data production and keeping the national topographic database current.
method: A web-based updating system was designed using OGC spatial web standards (WMS, WFS, WFS-T) to allow institutions to access, insert, update, and delete TOPOVT features over the network. UML was used for system modeling, and quality assurance mechanisms include feature-level metadata, 10% data sampling, and periodic revision by the General Command of Mapping via stereo imagery or field completion.
application_domain: Topographic mapping, national geospatial data management, and GIS applications for urban planning, defense, and environmental monitoring in Turkey
results_summary: The paper describes the design and implementation of the TOPOVT Real Time Updating System, which provides public institutions and municipalities direct internet-based access to the national topographic vector database via OGC web services. The system enables institutions to update features in their service areas, report errors and omissions, and share data, thereby eliminating duplicate geospatial data production nationwide. Quality assurance is addressed through feature-level metadata, a 10% sampling-based quality control, and periodic revision by the General Command of Mapping. The paper identifies challenges such as interoperability between different institutional data formats and the need for a mutually agreed schema, and proposes future extensions including Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI) via mobile phones and a multi-resolution database for urban areas.
limitations: Governmental institutions have historically gathered geospatial data in different formats and models, making interoperability between them very difficult; The success of the system critically depends on the mutual will of all shareholders to cooperate; Quality assurance initially requires users to obtain a certificate before they can begin contributing data
research_gaps: Further studies should discuss the outputs of the system in more detail; Refinements to the TOPOVT Real Time Updating System need to be developed; Improvements should be made to allow Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI) from Turkish citizens via mobile phones to contribute observations to a condensed version of TOPOVT; A multi-resolution database design is needed to achieve accuracy and resolution greater than 1:5,000 scale in urban areas

research_focus: Proposing a mathematical model based on directed graphs and matrix algebra to detect and remove superficial redundancy in vector databases, with an automated tool for computing redundancy levels and cleaning the database.
method: The vector database is modeled as an oriented directed graph characterized by an adjacency matrix over B = {0, 1}. Superficial redundancy is measured and filtered using the 1-norm of the matrix. Algorithms are implemented in Python and MapReduce, and the tool (RTRR) allows recovering the original or filtered database at any point in the process.
application_domain: Cybersecurity report databases (cleaning multi-source cybersecurity incident data)
results_summary: The paper develops a graph-theoretic model in which a vector database is represented by an adjacency matrix, and the level of superficial redundancy is quantified via the 1-norm of that matrix. An open-source tool called RTRR was implemented in Python and MapReduce to automate the detection and removal of redundant records and variables. When applied to a real multi-source cybersecurity database, the tool identified approximately 64% of the data as superficially redundant, indicating that roughly two-thirds of the records could be removed without loss of analytical value. The approach also permits recovering either the original or the filtered database at any stage of the cleaning process.
limitations: The model only addresses superficial redundancy (empty, constant, and identical cases) and does not handle deep redundancy such as correlated or non-discriminant variables; The tool RTRR lacks a graphical interface, limiting its accessibility to non-expert users; The tool is not available as an online version, restricting deployment in certain environments
research_gaps: Model additional types of redundancy, particularly deep redundancies (correlated variables, non-discriminant features); Develop a graphical interface for RTRR to make the tool more accessible to non-expert users; Create an online version of the RTRR tool

research_focus: Designing and implementing an efficient geospatial database updating system for the Turkish Topographic Vector Database (TOPOVT) that combines WMS service display with limited direct database connection, enabling rapid updates without losing information content or topological integrity.
method: A hybrid system was designed in three components: (1) a WMS service to display appropriate data images at desired scales, (2) a personal vector database on the user side for performing add, update, and delete operations, and (3) linking software connecting the WMS publication with the vector data structure. Two independent enterprise database systems with short-interval synchronization and dual WMS broadcasts over a single address provide redundancy. The system was implemented as a plugin for ArcGIS.
mentioned_systems: TOPOVT; Esri ArcGIS; QGIS; SAGA; GRASS
application_domain: Topographic mapping and geospatial data management (1:25,000 and higher scale 3D topographic vector data covering Turkey)
results_summary: The paper presents a hybrid WMS-and-direct-connection system for updating the TOPOVT geospatial database, addressing the slowdown caused by loading all vector data into GIS software for large-scale national datasets. The system uses two synchronized enterprise database systems with redundant WMS broadcasts, allowing users to view data via WMS while performing edits in temporary local files, then sending updates back to the enterprise database. Metadata fields (updater, source, source date, update date) are automatically populated to preserve historical records. The system was implemented as an ArcGIS plugin and is noted as conceptually compatible with open-source GIS software such as QGIS, SAGA, and GRASS for broader adoption in large geospatial data producer organizations.
limitations: Establishing a direct vector database link in ArcGIS loads all geodata onto the screen, causing slowdown in both display and update operations for large datasets; The system was developed using ArcGIS libraries (licensed software), limiting immediate applicability in environments that rely on open-source GIS tools; The high cost of licensed GIS software constrains the number of data producers that can be supported in web-based updating systems

research_focus: Finding the most suitable variables for detecting grassland to cropland land cover change using a pair of high-resolution Landsat 8 satellite images and the Land Parcel Identification System (LPIS) vector database as reference data.
method: Fifty-nine variables (spectral bands, vegetation indices, textures, Principal Component Analysis, Tasselled Cap components) were evaluated using Generalised Linear Models (GLM). Model quality was verified through multi-temporal object-based change detection against the LPIS reference database for the 2013–2016 period in the Czech Republic.
application_domain: Land use and land cover (LULC) change detection, specifically grassland-to-cropland transitions, with applications in landscape management, agriculture, and agricultural subsidy policy in Central Europe.
results_summary: The study tested 59 variables in GLM-based models and verified them through object-based multi-temporal change detection. A three-variable model combining NDVI, Wetness, and the Fifth component of Tasselled Cap was identified as the best practical compromise for accuracy and interpretability. Increasing the number of variables beyond three did not significantly improve detection accuracy and instead complicated result interpretation. Spectral variables proved more important than textural ones, and the timing of satellite image acquisition was confirmed as a critical factor. The authors conclude that the three-variable model is near the maximum accuracy achievable from a single pair of high-resolution multi-spectral images.

research_focus: Improving the performance of Asymmetric Distance Computation (ADC) in Product Quantization-based approximate nearest neighbor search by leveraging AVX-512 SIMD instructions, specifically addressing the challenge of efficiently using 5-, 6-, and 7-bit shuffles that do not align to computer bytes or words.
method: Quicker ADC introduces (i) irregular product quantizers combining sub-quantizers of different granularity (e.g., m×{6,6,4}, m×{8,8}) and (ii) split tables allowing lookup tables larger than registers. The implementation is integrated into FAISS and evaluated against reference optimized implementations (FAISS PQ and polysemous codes) across multiple index types (simple inverted index, IMI, IVF HNSW) on SIFT1000M and Deep1B datasets.
indexing_methods: HNSW; IVF; IMI; IVF HNSW; Product Quantization; ADC; PQ Fast Scan; polysemous codes
application_domain: Multimedia retrieval, including image similarity search, classification, and object recognition using high-dimensional feature descriptors (SIFT, GIST, deep-learning-based).
results_summary: Quicker ADC was implemented as an open-source fork of FAISS and evaluated against reference PQ and polysemous code implementations across multiple index types and datasets. Quicker ADC consistently outperforms polysemous codes, the state-of-the-art for fast response time, in both exhaustive and non-exhaustive search settings. For example, on SIFT1000M with a 0.25 ms query budget and 128-bit codes, Quicker ADC achieves R@100 of 0.68 with IVF HNSW versus 0.36 for polysemous codes. The m×{8,8} variant offers good recall with significantly reduced query times for exhaustive search, while m×{4,4} and m×{6,6,4} variants excel in non-exhaustive search when fast queries are desired. The authors note that upcoming processors with 7-bit shuffle support and dual shuffle units will further improve performance without algorithmic changes.

research_focus: Automatic road centerline correction/extraction from post-earthquake aerial images, using OpenStreetMap vector data as a constraint to overcome geo-localization and projection errors in free road datasets.
method: A road centerline correction method that uses context features and spectral gradient features of post-event aerial images under the constraint of OpenStreetMap vector road data. A road energy model implemented in a circle template considers road homogeneity, spectral features, and morphological gradient to rectify centerlines automatically without manual intervention.
application_domain: Post-earthquake road network extraction and correction from very high resolution remote sensing aerial images for disaster relief and reconstruction.
results_summary: The proposed automatic road centerline correction method was evaluated on 0.5 m/pixel post-event aerial images of Haiti (2010 earthquake). The method achieved over 90% completeness and over 80% extraction quality without any manual intervention. It was compared against two semiautomatic methods (a KDE/mean shift approach by Miao and a circle template method by Tan). The road energy model in a circle template was shown to better overcome the impact of building collapse, stains, and vehicles on the road compared to existing approaches.
limitations: When there are direction errors from the original vector data (OpenStreetMap), the proposed method will not spare from mistakes; The method has not yet been validated across various scenarios with different spatial resolutions
research_gaps: More experiments on various scenarios with different spatial resolution are needed to further prove the method's effectiveness; Fully automatic road centerline extraction remains unresolved, as existing algorithms are not robust to larger complex traffic scenes

research_focus: The paper addresses the need for advanced tools to automatically analyze satellite images and extract their full semantic content, specifically for coastal environmental monitoring. It outlines a highly automated data-mining and content interpretation system and applies it to three use cases in European UNESCO-protected coastal areas.
method: A five-component system is described: Data Sources (image selection and storage), Data Model Generation (patch cutting and feature vector extraction), Database Management System (data storage), Knowledge Discovery in Databases (clustering and content labeling), and Statistical Analytics (classification map generation). Images from TerraSAR-X, Sentinel-1, and Sentinel-2 are tiled into patches, feature vectors are extracted per sensor type, and classification is performed to assign semantic labels.
mentioned_systems: Tomnod; Google Earth; LandEX; GeoIRIS; IKONA; KIM; TELEIOS; CANDELA; Java 8; Matlab R2105a
application_domain: Coastal environmental monitoring via satellite image analysis: detection of wind turbines vs. boats, identification of fish cages/aquaculture, and classification of beaches, dams, dunes, and tidal flats in European protected areas.
results_summary: The authors developed and applied a five-component data-mining and content interpretation system to three use cases in European coastal protected areas (Wadden Sea, Mediterranean coast near Corfu, Danube Delta). Classification accuracy ranged from 80% to 95% depending on the sensor type, with higher-resolution instruments like TerraSAR-X yielding better results than medium-resolution Sentinel-1. The system runs on a desktop PC with less than 25% CPU usage and classifies new patches in approximately 4–6 ms for a 2 GB image collection. The authors conclude that higher-resolution products enable better identification of target categories and that semantic fusion of classification maps across different sensor types is possible.
limitations: Not all aquaculture features are visible in every image product due to sensor type (SAR vs. multi-spectral), resolution, and feature extraction methods; Classification accuracy varies significantly (80%–95%) depending on the image type and sensor resolution; Higher resolution is required to better identify areas of interest with higher accuracy

research_focus: Analysis of the slope (declivity) of the cycling network in the city of São Paulo to determine which segments are suitable for cycling (slopes ≤ 5%) and which are critical (slopes > 5%), using geoprocessing resources.
method: Two geoprocessing strategies were applied: (1) intersection of the vector data of the cycling network with a pre-existing slope map (carta de declividade), and (2) generation of a digital elevation model (DEM) from contour lines followed by assignment of altimetric/slope information to 100 m segments of the cycling network using ArcGIS surface tools.
application_domain: Urban cycling infrastructure and sustainable urban mobility (geospatial analysis of cycling network slopes)
results_summary: The paper applied two geoprocessing strategies to assess the declivity of approximately 742 km of cycling infrastructure in São Paulo. The first strategy (slope map intersection) indicated that 47% of the network had slopes above 5%, while the second strategy (DEM-based) found only 17.9% above 5%, a difference attributed to the much coarser scale of the slope map (1:100,000) versus the cycling network (1:1,000). The DEM-based method was judged more accurate because it used interpolation to compute exact slope values and matched the scale of the network data. Overall, the majority of the cycling network was found to have non-critical slopes (≤ 5%), facilitating cycling access. No clear spatial pattern of critical versus non-critical segments was identified across the city.
limitations: The slope map used in the first strategy has a much lower scale (1:100,000) than the cycling network data (1:1,000), which may have caused distortions in the intersection results.; Results from the slope map are conditioned to discrete slope classes, making it impossible to determine the exact slope value of individual cycling segments.; No in-situ (field) validation of the computed slopes was performed.; Comparative analysis using other topographic databases (e.g., Google Earth) was deemed outside the scope of the paper.
research_gaps: In-situ observation of the cycling paths would be needed for effective validation of the computed slopes.; A comparative analysis of declivities using other topographic databases (e.g., Google Earth) could be performed but was not carried out.; The DEM-based method for determining cycling network slopes could be applied to other urban centers, provided topographic and cycling network data are available.

research_focus: Improving position estimation accuracy for underground coal mine roadway localization by proposing a feature vector-matching algorithm (FVMA) that reduces multipath effects and improves real-time performance.
method: The FVMA algorithm consists of three steps: (1) constructing a feature vector database and a distance database by selecting seed vectors, iterating to divide samples into subsets, and pre-computing distances to subset center vectors; (2) vector matching by calculating the distance from the received signal vector to each subset's center vector to identify the relevant subset; (3) localization by filtering and comparing the strongest signal source among candidate vectors to determine the closest coordinate.
application_domain: Coal mine underground personnel localization and disaster rescue in roadway environments
results_summary: The FVMA algorithm was evaluated in a simulated 400 m coal mine roadway with 21 WiFi APs and 2000 training points. The maximum localization error was 4 m and the average error was 1.62 m. Within a 1 m error threshold, X-axis localization accuracy reached 98% while Y-axis accuracy was 86%. The algorithm demonstrated significantly lower computation time compared to KNN and WKNN, and effectively reduced the multipath effect without increasing hardware cost. The authors concluded that FVMA meets the accuracy and real-time requirements of coal mine safety and underground personnel localization systems.
limitations: The Y-axis localization error was slightly larger than the X-axis error, though the authors noted this was acceptable given the limited roadway width

research_focus: Evaluating the spatial accessibility of the population to hospital infrastructure in the North-West Region of Romania, identifying areas of deficit in access to various hospital categories (city, clinical, teaching, emergency).
method: A GIS Cost Surface Modeling approach to calculate access time from any location in the territory to the nearest hospital, using vector data layers (access ways, hospitals), assignment attributes (speed of motion on access ways, hospital type), and raster data (access time).
application_domain: Healthcare infrastructure accessibility evaluation and hospital network planning at regional scale
results_summary: The paper applied a GIS cost surface model to quantify access time to hospitals across the six counties of North-West Romania. Results showed that emergency hospitals, despite being present in every county capital, leave most localities with access times exceeding 30 minutes, and specialized emergency hospitals (cardiovascular, children's) are accessible only from Cluj-Napoca. Non-emergency hospitals show better accessibility, with city hospitals averaging 101.3 minutes and recovery hospitals the worst at 368.1 minutes. Areas of deficit were concentrated near Baia Mare, Satu Mare, Bistrița, and in mountainous or peripheral zones with poor road infrastructure. The authors conclude that the results can inform administrative decisions and suggest future studies to identify locations for new hospitals, patient transport units, and heliports.
research_gaps: Identifying potential locations for the establishment of new hospital units; Identifying possible locations for the establishment of patient transport units and heliports to compensate for difficult road accessibility

research_focus: Assessment of the spatial accuracy of building footprints in OpenStreetMap by comparing them with the reference dataset TOPOVT (Turkey Topographic Vector Database), and evaluation of two polygon-matching methods (centroid and overlap) for identifying corresponding buildings in urban and rural areas of Ankara, Turkey.
method: Matching buildings between OSM and TOPOVT were identified using two approaches: the Centroid Method (centroid of an OSM polygon falls inside a TOPOVT polygon) and the Overlap Method (polygons intersect). For matched buildings, the Hausdorff Distance was calculated to quantify spatial deviation. The methodology was applied to two ~150 km² regions (one urban, one rural) in Ankara, and an ArcGIS extension was developed to implement the workflow.
mentioned_systems: OpenStreetMap; ArcGIS; TOPOVT; Google Maps; Garmin
application_domain: Geospatial data quality assessment, specifically spatial accuracy of building footprints in Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI) datasets
results_summary: The paper applied the centroid and overlap matching methods to urban and rural regions in Ankara, Turkey, and computed Hausdorff distances for matched buildings. In the urban environment, both methods detected approximately 600 matching buildings out of 1123 in the reference dataset, with an average Hausdorff distance of about 9.5 meters. The centroid method was found to be marginally superior in the urban setting due to lower maximum Hausdorff distances, lower standard deviation, and shorter execution time. In the rural area, very few matches were found (only 20 OSM polygons vs. six times more in TOPOVT), making reliable conclusions difficult, and the centroid method effectively failed. The results support existing evidence that rural areas are underrepresented in VGI data.
limitations: No data cleaning or preprocessing step was carried out before the analysis; Only one-to-one building matches were investigated; one-to-many intersections were resolved by selecting the polygon with the lowest Hausdorff distance; The reference dataset (TOPOVT) dates back to 2011, while OSM data are more recent, introducing temporal mismatch; Very low number of matching buildings in the rural area makes it difficult to draw reliable conclusions; The centroid method failed in the rural environment
research_gaps: Analyze one-to-many polygon matching situations in more detail; Evaluate the effectiveness of different data cleaning and pre-processing strategies; Investigate the spatial accuracy of roads in a similar manner; Develop new ways to enrich VGI content in rural areas to enable more reliable accuracy assessments; Conduct further experimentation to support or refute the suggestion of preferring the centroid method

research_focus: The monthly variation and spatial distribution of quadrant tropical cyclone (TC) size (both symmetric and asymmetric structures) in the Western North Pacific, and the impact of climatological mean atmospheric circulation on quadrant TC size.
method: TC size was defined as the radius of 17 m/s oceanic surface wind, derived from the QuikSCAT near-surface wind vector database and a best-track dataset for 225 TC cases (2000–2009). TCs were classified into symmetric and asymmetric structures using a symmetry index (ratio of minimum to maximum quadrant sizes), and asymmetric TCs were further divided into four quadrant types (NE, SE, SW, NW). Monthly variation, spatial distribution, lifetime, and background circulation patterns were analyzed for each type.
application_domain: Tropical cyclone size analysis and atmospheric circulation studies in the Western North Pacific
results_summary: The study derived 1,229 TC size parameters from 225 TCs and found that the four asymmetric quadrant types exhibit distinct monthly and spatial patterns: NE-type cases peak in July and October across the WNP, SE-type peaks in July west of 155°E, SW-type is larger from June to August east of the Philippine Islands, and NW-type shows consistent size-lifetime changes near East Asian coasts. Lifetime and atmospheric circulation were identified as important factors affecting quadrant size. Four kinds of regional circulation patterns were described that correlate with the four asymmetric types, though overlapping regions complicate attribution. The relationship between relative SST and TC size was found to be not apparent across the WNP overall but showed a positive relationship in the specific region 15–30°N, 120–140°E where the climatological mean circulation was weakest.

research_focus: Converting Global Urban Footprint (GUF) raster data into vector databases for Polish settlements, including methods of data generalization, optimization of time and disk space, and combining with existing Polish geospatial databases.
method: GUF raster data were converted to vector form and divided into fragments according to administrative boundaries from BDOT10k. Mathematical morphology (closing followed by opening operations) was applied for generalization to reduce detail. The resulting databases were enriched with descriptive data from the National Geodetic and Cartographic Resource.
mentioned_systems: GUF; BDOT10k; BDOO; GHSL; PRG; Sentinel-1; Sentinel-2
application_domain: Urban settlement mapping, geospatial analysis, and settlement network monitoring in Poland
results_summary: The study developed two vector databases from GUF data: one at approximately 12 m resolution matching the original, and a second at approximately 20 m resolution generalized using mathematical morphology. research_focus: Analysis of soil parameters (physical, geographic, qualitative, production potential) characterizing four agricultural land use types (arable land, permanent grassland, vineyards, orchards) in Slovakia, and forecasting their future area development.
method: Geographic information system (ArcGIS) tools for spatial quantification and representation of vector soil parameter databases from the Soil Science and Conservation Research Institute, combined with exponential smoothing and Box-Jenkins (ARIMA) time series modeling for forecasting land use development.
application_domain: Agricultural land use analysis, soil science, and spatial planning in Slovakia
results_summary: The paper analyzed soil parameters of four agricultural land use types in Slovakia using GIS tools and vector soil parameter databases, finding that arable land (production potential 67 points) is located on plains, permanent grassland (35 points) on higher slopes with gravel, vineyards (59 points) in warm southern regions, and orchards (63 points) on plains. Exponential smoothing and ARIMA forecasting confirmed a continuing decline in arable land (approx. 2020 ha), permanent grassland (approx. 5580 ha), and vineyards (approx. 190 ha) by 2024, with a slight increase in orchards (approx. 140 ha). The study found that not all soils are used in accordance with their productive potential, with some steep, gravelly, or shallow soils being used as arable land. The results indicate that Slovakia's share of agricultural land (48.6%) is higher than the European average, but the overall trend shows a gradual decline in agricultural soils since 1950.
limitations: Existing simulation models, computer packages for land assessment in spatial planning, and economic models of land use are largely incorrect and give inaccurate results when applied to local conditions unless specifically calibrated for that region; A more detailed description of soil parameters as limits for soil use is absent in statistical reviews, both in Slovakia and globally; More detailed analysis of soil conditions at specific sites is scarce in existing literature
research_gaps: Further research and forecasting in the field of agricultural land use development and soil parameter analysis is needed; Government policy should devote more attention to expanding orchards and vineyards, for instance through systemic subsidies

research_focus: Proposing a biometric-driven facial image recognition method based on multivariate correlation analysis that combines geometrical feature points (via Active Shape Model) and low-level visual features (colour and texture), with comparison performed against a feature vector database using the Canonical Correlation method.
method: Geometrical features are extracted using Active Shape Model (ASM); colour features are extracted from the YCbCr colour model; texture features are extracted via the autocorrelation method. The extracted features are formed into a feature tensor matrix and compared to stored feature matrices in a feature vector database using the Canonical Correlation (CCC) method at various significance levels (1% to 40%).
application_domain: Biometric authentication and facial image recognition
results_summary: The paper proposes a facial recognition method combining ASM-based geometrical features with YCbCr colour and autocorrelation-based texture features, compared via Canonical Correlation against a feature vector database. Experiments on GT, LFW, Pointing '04, and a custom celebrity dataset yielded mean precision scores (mP@a) of 95.27%, 94.20%, 96.19%, and 96.05% respectively. The optimal significance level was determined to be 15% (α=0.15), achieving an mP@a of 98.17%. F-scores ranged from 95.15% to 97.08% across datasets. The results were found to be comparable to existing methods such as KPM and CRRF.
limitations: At the 1% significance level, the system fails to detect similar (but not identical) images, returning no result if the exact key image is absent from the database

research_focus: Key-frame detection and video retrieval using DC coefficient-based cosine orthogonality and multivariate parametric statistical tests for matching feature vectors between a query key-frame and a feature vector database.
method: Background and foreground are separated via a colour intensity-based algorithm; salient features (colour and Gabor texture) are extracted from both components and formulated as a feature vector. Matching is performed using multivariate parametric statistical tests: first a test for equality of covariance matrices, and if passed, a test for equality of mean vectors. The optimal significance threshold was determined experimentally at α = 0.15.
application_domain: Video retrieval, key-frame detection, and background/foreground segmentation in multimedia content
results_summary: The paper proposes a video retrieval method that separates background and foreground, extracts colour and Gabor texture features, and matches them using multivariate parametric statistical tests. research_gaps: Extension of the technique to big-data analytics with multiple characteristics for both offline and online data analytics; Refinement of the method and implementation of online video analysis and retrieval

research_focus: The insufficient exploration of competitive endogenous RNA (ceRNA) regulatory networks comprising miRNAs, lncRNAs, and mRNAs in Uveal Melanoma, and the need for an integrated, accessible tool to identify and visualize these RNA-RNA relationships.
method: Integration of TCGA-derived expression correlation values (miRNA-mRNA, miRNA-lncRNA, lncRNA-mRNA pairs) with predicted and validated RNA-RNA interactions, sense-antisense sequence overlapping data, and transcription factor regulatory correlations (with ChIPseq data) into an interactive web-based database with graph visualization and expression heatmaps.
application_domain: Cancer genomics and RNA signaling in Uveal Melanoma, specifically ceRNA network analysis involving miRNAs, lncRNAs, and mRNAs
results_summary: The authors built VECTOR, an interactive web-based database that integrates TCGA-derived expression correlations among miRNAs, lncRNAs, and mRNAs with predicted and validated RNA-RNA interactions, sense-antisense overlapping data, and transcription factor regulatory information for Uveal Melanoma. The database allows users to query by gene name and visualize ceRNA networks as interactive graphs with associated expression heatmaps, reducing the time and expertise previously needed for such analyses. Validation against literature confirmed several predicted molecular axes, including the LINC00518/miR-199a-5p sponge interaction and multiple transcription factor regulatory loops (CREB1, GABPA, JUND, MAZ, RELA, SOX2, SPI1). Analysis of sense-antisense pairs confirmed that positive expression correlation is most common in divergent pairs (over 80%), while negative correlation is more frequent in convergent pairs (28.3% vs. 16.8%). The authors demonstrated that VECTOR provides a comprehensive and accessible view of ceRNA networks in UM, making tumor-related ceRNA circuits available to non-expert biocomputational researchers.
limitations: The UM TCGA dataset includes only tumor tissue samples and lacks physiological tissue data, making tumor-versus-normal differential expression analysis impossible; Stratification of tumor samples by clinicopathological features would create subgroups with too few samples, impairing statistical power, so stratified analyses were not performed; Multiple splicing variants of sense and antisense transcripts created a complex and heterogeneous scenario in which no clear classification of overlapping regions (introns vs. exons) was possible
research_gaps: The exact molecular mechanism underlying the co-regulation or inverse correlation of sense and antisense transcripts is still under investigation; The VECTOR approach could be extended to build similar tools for other cancer models to make tumor-related ceRNA circuits accessible to non-expert researchers; The etiology of Uveal Melanoma remains unclear, and the contribution of non-coding RNAs to its pathogenesis is still insufficiently understood

research_focus: Soil classification and agricultural potentiality assessment for rainfed areas in the El-Qasr – Um El-Rakham region at the northwestern coast of Egypt, covering 12 drainage basins and approximately 159,603 feddan.
method: Spatial identification of landforms using geological and topographic maps integrated with DEM; soil profile distribution based on ETM+ LANDSAT 7 image classification; survey of 261 soil profiles with 24 representative profiles selected; creation of a digital vector database using GIS; soil classification following Soil Survey Staff (SSS, 2010) taxonomy; and generation of soil and evaluation maps.
application_domain: Soil classification, landform delineation, and agricultural land capability assessment in a desert/rainfed region of Egypt
results_summary: The study identified six main landform units and ten soil mapping units differentiated by profile depth, texture, and topography. research_focus: The relationship between Sky View Factor (SVF) and Land Surface Temperature (LST) at different spatial and temporal scales, including seasonal variation, day-night variation, and the impact of building height and density on the SVF-LST relationship.
method: SVF was calculated using a geometric method based on a building vector database, and LST was retrieved from Landsat-8 and ASTER thermal infrared satellite imagery. The SVF-LST relationship was analyzed across four periods in 2018 in the core built-up area of Beijing, with additional analysis of building shadow ratios in three building-height categories at 30 m and 90 m pixel scales.
application_domain: Urban thermal environment analysis and urban morphology assessment using remote sensing
results_summary: The study addressed the SVF-LST relationship by computing continuous SVF from a building vector database and retrieving LST from Landsat-8 and ASTER thermal infrared data over Beijing's core built-up area. Results showed that SVF and LST are positively correlated at night, while the daytime relationship varies with image scale and season. Nonlinear fitting at 30 m scale yielded better results than at 90 m scale, and the shadow cooling effect around buildings was identified as a contributing factor. The average building shadow ratio was largest (0.38) in mid-rise building areas in winter, and LST was lower in areas with higher shaded coverage. The findings indicate that the SVF-LST relationship is modulated by spatial scale, season, building height, and shading effects.
limitations: Vegetation and water interference were ignored during statistical analysis of the SVF-LST relationship; Only SVF and building shadow ratio were used to analyze the influence of 3D building structure on LST, without considering other environmental factors; The analysis did not account for different building functions that produce different anthropogenic heat
research_gaps: Further studies should consider the influence of the joint building functional area and the surrounding environment on land surface temperature; The effect of different building functions producing different anthropogenic heat on the SVF-LST relationship needs to be investigated

research_focus: The paper evaluates the use of the SOPO landslide database in local spatial planning (LSDP) in mountain communes of the Polish Carpathians, examining the co-occurrence of landslides with existing and planned residential development in 14 selected communes.
method: The study cross-references existing vector databases (SOPO landslide inventory, BDOT building database, and LSDP planning data) to quantify the spatial overlap between landslide areas and residential/planned development zones (M1-3) in 14 communes, and assesses the quality of spatial planning decisions in light of known landslide hazards.
mentioned_systems: SOPO (Landslide Counteracting System); BDOT (Database of Topographic Objects); Geo-System
application_domain: Spatial planning and landslide hazard risk assessment in mountainous regions (Polish Carpathians)
results_summary: The study demonstrated a high natural landslide hazard in the 14 analysed communes, with landslides covering 1–23% of commune area and up to 11% of M1-3 development areas. A total of 722 buildings were recorded in M1-3 areas occupied by landslides, and 10–23% of gross floor area in 17 Carpathian communes was located in landslide zones. The analysis revealed faulty spatial planning: even after the SOPO database was established, LSDPs in the vast majority of communes (12 out of 14) did not adequately account for landslide hazards, with no statistically significant difference in landslide-affected M1-3 area between plans created before and after SOPO. research_focus: Cross-time matching and retrieval of geographical areas (specifically vertical aerial photographs) by encoding geographic entities and their spatial relationships as attributed graphs and learning graph embeddings for similarity search, addressing the challenge that visual appearance changes over time and across seasons.
method: A Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) in a Siamese-like architecture is used to learn compact graph embeddings of geographic areas. Geographic entities (buildings, roads, watercourses, etc.) are represented as nodes with geometric and semantic attributes, and their spatial relationships as edges. Training uses contrastive learning on known correspondences, and retrieval is performed via KNN search over the learned embeddings. Two original datasets (same-source and cross-source) are created from topographic vector databases (IGN, OSM) for evaluation.
application_domain: Historical aerial photograph retrieval, geospatial data matching, GIS-based territorial analysis, and cross-time geographic area indexing for historians and archivists working with large volumes of historical visual sources.
results_summary: The paper proposes GisGCN, a GCN-based Siamese framework for learning graph embeddings of geographic areas, and creates two original cross-time and cross-source datasets as the first benchmark of their kind. The GCN-based model is currently outperformed by an unsupervised attribute-similarity baseline in map@5 scores, but demonstrates significantly greater robustness to attribute noise (10% decrease vs. 70% decrease for the Faiss-based baseline). For same-source data, the model achieves correct matches in more than 50% of queries across time gaps of up to 15 years. Cross-source and cross-time results are substantially lower, indicating the model does not yet generalize well to unseen data sources. The authors conclude the approach is a promising new research direction for geographical graph matching despite not yet matching classical methods.
limitations: The GCN-based model is currently outperformed by the unsupervised attribute-similarity baseline in map@5 scores; The model does not generalize well to cross-source data, with quite low map@5 values; The training procedure is under-specified and the model does not generalize well to new data; The approach requires segmentation as a prior step, which is not straightforward for aerial photographs or ancient maps; The maximum number of nodes in a single graph is artificially limited to 150; Graphs with fewer than 3 nodes were excluded from the dataset; The approach is not generalizable enough at the current state for cross-source matching; The graph architecture and network parameters are highly interdependent with no clear trend discovered
research_gaps: Improve the efficiency of the matching models; Study different matching architectures; Adapt the GCN so it can handle graphs of different sizes; Apply the model to new application domains; Adopt an attention mechanism in the graph models; Improve the graph representation to achieve better retrieval results; Encode textual features such as toponyms as additional graph nodes; Use object detection methods to obtain graph nodes instead of relying on pre-segmented vector data; Extend the approach to matching across oblique aerial image sets; Exploit image and vectorial data together in a unified framework

research_focus: Efficient organization and management of large vector map data for rendering on global 3D terrain surfaces in 3D GIS, addressing the inefficiency of traditional vector database schemes and the detail loss of texture tiled pyramid approaches.
method: The authors propose the Vector Tiled Pyramid Model (VTPM), in which vector data at different scales within the same geographical extent are stored as separate levels, each divided into fixed-size vector tiles organized in a grid index. A prototype system was built to visualize vector data on 3D terrain surfaces based on the VTPM, and its performance was compared against a traditional vector database scheme.
mentioned_systems: ArcSDE; Oracle Spatial; Web Map Tile Service
application_domain: 3D GIS visualization of large vector maps on global 3D terrain surfaces
results_summary: The paper proposes the Vector Tiled Pyramid Model (VTPM) to organize vector data into hierarchical levels of fixed-size tiles arranged in a grid index, enabling efficient access by bypassing irrelevant data entities. A prototype system was built and experimental results show that, compared with a traditional vector database scheme, the VTPM enables faster access to vector data for visualization on 3D terrain surfaces. The efficiency advantage is more pronounced when lower-level (large-scale) vector tiles are requested. Unlike texture tiled pyramids, VTPM vector tiles can be rendered using geometry-based, texture-based, or combined approaches, achieving a better balance between rendering efficiency and visual quality.
limitations: The topology of vector data is undermined due to the partitioning into tiles; Spatial analysis of vector data within the VTPM is a problem
research_gaps: Building and incorporating a more extensive indexing structure to preserve topological relationships among vector objects in the VTPM
