research_focus: Development of a general, modular AI framework that integrates sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and abstractive summarization for automated analysis of textual user reviews, validated through a cultural heritage case study on a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
method: A modular architecture rooted in the MVC paradigm combining DistilBERT for sentiment analysis, FASTopic for topic modeling, and Gemini Flash 2.0 for abstractive summarization, supported by vector databases and caching mechanisms for scalability. The framework was instantiated as VisitorLens AI for Google Maps reviews of Kotor Fortress and evaluated through both quantitative NLP metrics and a qualitative expert questionnaire.
mentioned_systems: DistilBERT; FASTopic; BERTopic; Gemini Flash 2.0; VisitorLens AI; GPT; Gemini; BERT
application_domain: Cultural heritage management and tourism, specifically automated analysis of visitor reviews for a UNESCO World Heritage Site (Kotor Fortress, Montenegro)
results_summary: The paper proposed a unified AI framework integrating three NLP tasks (sentiment analysis, topic modeling, summarization) and validated it through the VisitorLens AI implementation on Google Maps reviews of Kotor Fortress. Quantitative evaluation confirmed high performance across NLP tasks, while the expert questionnaire showed 77% of ratings in the high range (4-5), with helpfulness at 81% high and factual correctness at 76% high. The system successfully identified UNESCO-relevant aspects, confirmed good practices (aesthetics, safety), and flagged gaps (architectural characteristics, continuity of tradition). The results demonstrated the framework's generalizability, robustness, and practical value for both tourists and local authorities in deriving actionable insights from unstructured review data.
limitations: Performance challenges during real-time processing of tasks like topic modeling; Lack of adaptive tuning based on user feedback, reducing ability to improve over time; Keyword-based queries may introduce subjectivity, resulting in narrow or less coherent summaries; Uniform user experience without specialized features for institutional users; Reliance on external APIs (e.g., Gemini Flash 2.0) introduces potential instability due to evolving third-party services; Pilot study with a moderate dataset for Kotor Fortress; Lacks native multilingual capabilities and depends on platform-based translations, which may lead to inconsistencies; Current focus on Google Maps reviews limits integration with other platforms and restricts broader data analysis; Limited number of available tourism and cultural heritage experts (seven) due to Kotor being a small historical town; Reviews represent opinions of a small, self-selected group of visitors based on particularly positive or negative experiences, potentially under-representing the average experience; Content tends to focus on immediate, visible aspects rather than deeper cultural or historical themes; Absence of institutional engagement on public platforms reduces opportunities for dialogue, clarification, and collaborative interpretation
research_gaps: Adaptive tuning based on user feedback to improve the system over time; Native multilingual capabilities to avoid inconsistencies from platform-based translations; Integration with review platforms beyond Google Maps for broader data analysis; Specialized features for institutional users beyond the current uniform user experience; Application of the general framework to diverse domains beyond cultural heritage (e.g., product evaluation)

research_focus: Developing a novel, cost-effective Machine Learning model for early COPD diagnosis using a comprehensive set of physical tests and risk factors, as an alternative to expensive and potentially unsafe imaging-based methods (CT/X-ray scans).

method: Comparative evaluation of open-source LLMs, embedding models, and vector databases to determine the optimal RAG configuration, followed by implementation of the system with responsive web technologies and evaluation using a standardized test question bank with McNemar's test for statistical validation.

results_summary: The paper developed CE-GAITA, a locally deployed RAG-based teaching assistant, by comparatively evaluating combinations of open-source LLMs, embedding models, and vector databases. Initial configurations using LLaMA3.2 and LLaVA with GPT4All and Hugging Face embeddings yielded accuracies of only 44.8%–60.5%, below the practical threshold. After screening, DeepSeek-r1:14b and Gemma3:12b were selected as core models, and the optimal configuration (DeepSeek-r1:14b + Hugging Face all-mpnet-base-v2 + ChromaDB) achieved 85.6% accuracy on quiz questions. RAG integration provided an average accuracy increase of 9.85% over the native LLM alone. The system was shown to be feasible as a privacy-preserving, scalable AI teaching aid in on-premise educational environments.
limitations: Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice items and does not involve direct participation from students or educators; Pedagogical claims remain theoretical and warrant empirical validation; RAG architecture cannot entirely eliminate the risk of hallucinations or fabricated output; Even occasional inaccuracies in educational settings can mislead learners if not properly managed

research_focus: Developing and evaluating a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that combines semantic vector retrieval with LLM generation to address hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and lack of domain adaptation in large language models.
method: The paper builds a RAG pipeline using Pinecone as a vector database, mixedbreadai embeddings for semantic similarity search, and Gemini-1.5-pro for text generation. Multiple chunking strategies are evaluated, prompt-tuning techniques are incorporated, and security threats such as prompt injection attacks are addressed.

application_domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), with references to enterprise, academic, healthcare, legal, and cybersecurity applications
results_summary: The paper developed a RAG system integrating Pinecone, mixedbreadai embeddings, and Gemini-1.5-pro, and evaluated it across multiple chunking strategies and prompt-tuning configurations. Results indicated improved factual accuracy, reduced hallucinations, and enhanced user trust compared to standalone LLM generation. Security considerations, including prompt injection attacks, were explicitly addressed within the framework. The authors conclude the system is suitable for real-world enterprise and academic applications.

research_gaps: Hybrid retrieval combining symbolic and neural approaches; Hierarchical retrieval frameworks such as RAPTOR; Integrating user feedback for explainable AI; Addressing both retrieval efficiency and system robustness simultaneously

research_focus: Enabling nontechnical users to query NoSQL (MongoDB) inventory databases through natural language by integrating LLM-based query generation with vector retrieval for semantic similarity matching, specifically targeting real-time inventory management applications.
method: The system uses transfer learning with Hugging Face Sentence-Transformer embeddings for query understanding, FAISS for vector-based semantic retrieval of relevant query examples, and few-shot prompting with LLaMA 3.3-70B (fine-tuned for MongoDB syntax) to generate optimized queries. Performance of various embedding techniques and vector search architectures (FAISS, ChromaDB, Annoy) is benchmarked for retrieval speed and accuracy.
mentioned_systems: FAISS; ChromaDB; Annoy; MongoDB; LLaMA 3.3-70B; Sentence-Transformer; GPT-4; DB-GPT; MongoNL; InvAgent
application_domain: Inventory management in retail and supply chain, specifically natural language querying of NoSQL (MongoDB) databases for stock levels, sales analysis, discounts, and product details
results_summary: The paper proposes and evaluates an LLM-augmented system that translates natural language queries into optimized MongoDB commands for inventory management. Among the tested vector databases, FAISS demonstrated the lowest query execution latency due to its parallelised search and optimised L2 distance calculation, outperforming ChromaDB and Annoy. The semantic retrieval-augmented few-shot learning approach achieved a cosine similarity score of 0.935, significantly improving query accuracy and reducing syntax errors to 2.5% (compared to 18% for the MongoNL baseline). The system effectively handles complex aggregation queries and nested filtering conditions while maintaining real-time performance. Overall, the integration of vector retrieval with LLM-based query generation enables nontechnical users to access structured inventory insights without requiring database expertise.
limitations: Performance deteriorates for deeply nested multi-collection aggregations, with syntax error rate increasing to 7%; Zero-shot scenario produces lower semantic match (0.826 cosine similarity) and requires more reliable prompt retrieval; Scalability to datasets larger than 10 million records has not yet been confirmed
research_gaps: Dynamic Schema Adaptation: use real-time schema reflection to ensure timely grounding; Interactive Clarification Dialogue: incorporate a two-turn question-answering module to clarify user intent; Advanced Retrieval Strategies: investigate cross-encoder model re-ranking for zero-shot improvements and hybrid ANN techniques (e.g., HNSW); Benchmark Integration: community leaderboard-based open-source assessment on Spider and WikiSQL

research_focus: Anomaly detection in time series data by integrating large language models with retrieval-augmented generation over a vector database, applied to real-world air quality monitoring.
method: A five-stage pipeline: (1) 1D U-Net segmentation of time series into candidate anomalous subsequences, (2) embedding via T-Rep (Huber loss) and retrieval of similar historical segments from a vector database, (3) spatial comparison across neighboring sensors using DTW and Z-score, (4) construction of structured prompts fusing retrieved evidence and statistical cues, (5) LLM-based decision generation with natural-language explanations.
application_domain: Air quality monitoring and environmental time series anomaly detection (CO, NO, NO2, O3, SO2 pollutant data from South Korea)
results_summary: The framework was evaluated on real-world hourly air quality data from South Korea (July–August 2024) covering five pollutants. Compared to a 1D U-Net segmentation-only baseline, the proposed method reduced total alarms by 52.9% and false positives by 54.9% (2,233 → 1,006) while preserving recall (88 vs. 89 true positives). The T-Rep encoder trained with Huber loss consistently outperformed TS2Vec and MSE-based T-Rep across precision and recall metrics. The proposed method achieved the best overall accuracy (0.93) and matched the 1D U-Net in total recall (0.84), outperforming six supervised sequence classifiers in this imbalanced real-world setting.
limitations: Findings are based on univariate hourly series from a single national network; generalization to other regions, sampling rates, or multivariate settings is not guaranteed; End-to-end performance remains sensitive to the initial segmentation stage because missed segments cannot be recovered downstream; Retrieval quality is bounded by encoder capacity and corpus coverage and may degrade under distribution shift; Faithfulness of LLM-generated explanations to evidence is not fully assured without additional controls; Large-scale embedding maintenance, DTW-based spatial scoring, and LLM prompting introduce compute and latency overheads
research_gaps: Extending the framework to multivariate time series; Assessing performance on complex anomaly types; Improving the consistency and diversity of LLM-generated explanations; Enhancing the scalability of vector retrieval operations; Conducting a comprehensive scalability analysis of the full pipeline

research_focus: Context-aware information retrieval for workers in Industry 5.0 / Internet of Everything (IoE) environments, where heterogeneous and dynamic industrial data must be efficiently retrieved and presented to operators. The paper proposes RAG-IoE, a hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation solution combining Knowledge Graph search with vector-database-based unstructured retrieval and LLM-driven reasoning.
method: The authors define a context-aware data model for IoE scenarios and build RAG-IoE, which organizes IoE data within a semantic framework. The retrieval pipeline combines structured search on a Knowledge Graph (used as a pre-filtering mechanism) with unstructured data retrieval using embeddings stored in a vector database, followed by LLM-driven reasoning to refine results. Validation is performed through a user study with two annotators and quantitative evaluation using the RAGAS suite (with Zephyr-7B as judge) on a novel manually-curated dataset combining real-world sensor information and LLM-generated natural language descriptions.
mentioned_systems: Llama-3.2-1B; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B; Qwen2.5-3B; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LlaMa-8B; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B; Zephyr-7B; RAGAS; GPT-4
application_domain: Industry 5.0 / IoT (Internet of Everything) industrial settings, specifically context-aware information retrieval for factory operators interacting with smart sensors, actuators, and machinery
results_summary: The paper proposes RAG-IoE, a hybrid RAG architecture that integrates a Knowledge Graph as a pre-filtering mechanism with vector-database-based embedding retrieval and LLM reasoning, and validates it on a novel IoE dataset. User-study results show that larger models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LlaMa-8B) achieve consistently strong accuracy, relevance, and usefulness across easy, medium, and hard activities, while smaller models (Llama-3.2-1B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) struggle significantly with complex multi-sensor reasoning tasks. 21% of generated responses contained hallucinated content and were excluded from final scoring. RAGAS-based quantitative evaluation with Zephyr-7B as judge provided additional benchmarking, though the authors note that RAG evaluation in highly specialized domains may yield suboptimal scores. Overall, the approach demonstrates that even relatively small LLMs on edge devices can generate meaningful, useful responses for factory operators when leveraging context from both the vector store and the operator's ego-network.
limitations: The evaluation does not include direct comparisons with existing RAG-based or graph-based methods; Adapting standard baselines to the hybrid architecture would require significant architectural changes and may be technically infeasible due to prompt size limitations; 21% of generated responses contained hallucinated content, reducing the pool of evaluable outputs; Smaller models (Llama-3.2-1B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) fail to generalize effectively on complex multi-sensor activities; For complex activities, models tend to generate lengthy and repetitive responses that list available machinery and sensors without effectively leveraging retrieved context; Models often fail to guide operators toward specific machinery and sensors using their unique identifiers, making responses harder to interpret
research_gaps: Direct comparison with existing RAG-based or graph-based retrieval methods to highlight the distinct advantages of the hybrid KG + vector-database architecture; Dynamic and adaptive visualization strategies for information generated by IoE systems, potentially using LLMs to generate analytics dashboards (e.g., Retrieval-Augmented Text-to-Image Generator); Identifying possible collaborations between agents, taking into account user expertise, activity complexity, and the physical/mental status or load level of involved agents (human employees or smart objects)

research_focus: Building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) powered chatbot that combines semantic vector-based retrieval with a large language model to provide accurate, context-aware answers to queries about complex university policy documents, along with a user feedback mechanism for continuous improvement.
method: A RAG architecture is implemented using FAISS as the vector store for similarity-based retrieval of document chunks (via embeddings), with the Grok LLM generating natural-language responses. A feedback mechanism allows users to rate or refine responses, enabling iterative system improvement.
application_domain: Conversational AI / NLP applied to institutional policy document enquiry in academic and administrative settings
results_summary: The paper addresses the challenge of accessing complex policy documents by implementing a RAG chatbot that integrates FAISS-based semantic retrieval with the Grok LLM for response generation. Document chunking and embeddings enable efficient retrieval of relevant policy sections even when users phrase queries in diverse natural language forms. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the system significantly improves query accuracy, reduces response time, and enhances user satisfaction compared to traditional keyword search or static FAQ approaches. The feedback mechanism provides a continuous improvement cycle, and the architecture is shown to be scalable to multiple departments, institutions, and document types.
research_gaps: Multilingual support; Advanced analytics; Integration with mobile platforms

research_focus: Automating incident diagnosis and resolution in cloud environments using a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system that combines Large Language Models with a domain-specific knowledge base built from code artifacts, logs, documentation, and historical tickets.
method: The authors design a RAG architecture that indexes heterogeneous operational data sources into a vector database, enabling LLMs to retrieve semantically relevant context before generating remediation suggestions. The knowledge base is continuously updated with deployment logs, API traces, and resolved incidents. Evaluation combines retrospective analysis on historical incidents and controlled experiments in production environments, measuring diagnostic accuracy, resolution time reduction, and operational safety.
application_domain: Cloud incident response, Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), and DevOps operations for microservice-based cloud infrastructure
results_summary: The RAG system was deployed in shadow mode across three production environments encompassing over 200 microservices, processing 732 distinct incidents over three months. Of these, 42% were fully resolved using the system's recommended actions without modification, 31% were resolved using modified recommendations, 18% required human investigation beyond the system's capabilities, and 9% received incorrect or potentially harmful recommendations. The system demonstrated significant potential for reducing Mean Time To Resolution and autonomously handling recurring incident types. However, LLM reasoning failures and hallucinations (4-11% for technical information) remained, particularly for novel failure modes not well-represented in training data. The authors conclude that domain-specific RAG systems can substantially reduce resolution times and automate remediation for common issues, while highlighting ongoing challenges in knowledge freshness, causal reasoning, and human trust calibration.
limitations: LLM component occasionally generates plausible but incorrect explanations for observed symptoms; Conflation of information from multiple similar but distinct incidents; Overconfidence in recommendations despite limited evidence; Hallucination rates of 4-11% when processing technical information, rising to 7-13% for novel concept combinations; Reasoning errors most frequent for incident types combining familiar components in unfamiliar ways; Issues most pronounced for novel failure modes not well-represented in training data; 9% of incidents received incorrect or potentially harmful recommendations that were rejected; Knowledge freshness challenges; Causal understanding of complex failures remains limited; Human trust calibration is an ongoing challenge
research_gaps: Improving knowledge freshness of the continuously updated knowledge base; Addressing fundamental reasoning limitations of LLMs in incident diagnosis; Developing better causal understanding of complex, multi-service failures; Calibrating human trust in automated recommendations; Reducing hallucination rates for novel failure modes and edge cases; Broader adoption and maturation of LLM-based observability tools in production

research_focus: Building a scalable, distributed vector database that achieves high throughput and high recall under concurrent read-write workloads, addressing three limitations of existing vector databases: computation overhead in high-dimensional spaces, read-write contention, and poor multi-server scalability.
method: A two-stage filter-and-refine ANN index (HAKES-Index) combining dimensionality reduction, 4-bit product quantization, and a lightweight machine learning technique to optimize compression parameters, with decoupled index parameters for search vs. insertion to support concurrent read-write workloads, deployed in a disaggregated distributed architecture (HAKES).
mentioned_systems: HAKES; FAISS; ScaNN; SPFresh; RoarGraph; OPQIVF-PQFS_RF
indexing_methods: IVF; PQ; HNSW; LVQ; OPQ; dimensionality reduction; graph-based indexes; partitioning-based indexes
application_domain: General-purpose approximate nearest neighbor search over high-dimensional deep learning embedding vectors, with applications in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), search engines, recommendation systems, and multi-modal (text-to-image) search.
results_summary: The authors propose HAKES-Index, a two-stage filter-and-refine index with learned compression parameters, and HAKES, a distributed vector database using a disaggregated architecture. They evaluate against 12 state-of-the-art indexes and 3 distributed vector databases on high-dimensional embedding datasets generated by deep learning models. HAKES-Index outperforms both partitioning-based and graph-based index baselines in the high recall region and under concurrent read-write workloads. HAKES achieves up to 16× higher throughput than the three distributed baselines at high recall. The system maintains stable recall (~0.99) under insertions and deletions, though throughput decreases with accumulated updates.
limitations: On low-dimensional datasets (e.g., SIFT with 128 dimensions), HAKES-Index falls behind some baselines such as HNSW and LVQ; The learning technique provides little improvement for low-dimensional vectors not generated by neural networks; Search throughput decreases after a large number of insertions and deletions due to additional vectors or tombstones to check during the filter stage; New vectors with distribution drift can impact the recall of HAKES-Index; As the dataset grows considerably, the index must be rebuilt with a larger number of IVF partitions; HAKES-Index is designed specifically for high-dimensional embedding vectors and is not optimal for low-dimensional data
research_gaps: Handling out-of-distribution (ODD) queries where query vectors and indexed data vectors come from different modalities (e.g., text queries vs. image embeddings) is identified as an emerging research problem; Efficiently managing index partitioning as the dataset grows significantly without full rebuilds remains a practical challenge

research_focus: Automated generation and classification of multiple-choice questions (MCQs) aligned with Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive levels, using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and a vector database, to support personalized cognitive assessment in education.
method: A 1D CNN neural network with transformer-based text embeddings (Specter and MathBERT) is used for Bloom's Taxonomy question classification. For question generation, a RAG framework combines the Gemini LLM with Chroma DB as a vector database to ensure pattern adherence. Cosine similarity is used to evaluate semantic closeness of generated questions to reference questions.
mentioned_systems: Gemini; Chroma DB; GPT-4o-mini; Specter; MathBERT
application_domain: Educational assessment and automated MCQ generation for cognitive-level-aligned learning
results_summary: The paper proposes and implements BT-GEN, a system that integrates Bloom's Taxonomy classification with RAG-based MCQ generation. For classification, Specter embeddings with a 1D CNN outperformed MathBERT, achieving a weighted F1-score of 0.53 versus 0.38, though both models struggled to distinguish higher-order levels such as Analyse, Evaluate, and Apply. For generation, the RAG pipeline using Gemini and Chroma DB produced contextually relevant MCQs, evaluated via cosine similarity against reference questions. The system also includes visualization tools for tracking question distribution and student performance, laying groundwork for cognitive profiling. Overall, the results demonstrate a functional end-to-end pipeline but reveal persistent challenges in fine-grained cognitive-level discrimination.
limitations: Training and testing datasets were small and domain-specific, limiting generalizability across different subjects or question types; Effectiveness of generated questions was evaluated only via cosine similarity scores, with no human-in-the-loop evaluation by teachers or subject experts; Cognitive profiling was only partially implemented; tracking question-solving time and generating personalized improvement suggestions were not fully realized
research_gaps: Curate a larger and more diverse dataset of questions across various domains, manually annotated with Bloom's levels, to improve model robustness; Fine-tune transformer models such as Specter or Sentence-BERT on Bloom's Taxonomy-specific question datasets to enhance semantic sensitivity and classification accuracy; Explore hybrid classification methods combining semantic embeddings with rule-based or syntactic features (e.g., question verbs, structure) to reduce misclassification between closely related Bloom levels; Incorporate expert reviews and rubric-based assessments of generated questions to validate cognitive level, clarity, and educational value; Implement remaining cognitive profiling components including tracking student response times, suggesting targeted improvements, and analysing learning progress over time; Fine-tune the retrieval and generation stages of the RAG pipeline using Bloom-level aligned corpora to enhance contextual relevance of generated questions

research_focus: Extending an IoT sensor setup assistance service (SEMAR platform) to handle unlearned sensors by extracting specifications from PDF datasheets using generative AI, storing them in a vector database via chunking and embedding, and leveraging Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to provide step-by-step setup guidance.
method: A four-step pipeline: (1) user inputs a PDF datasheet, (2) a generative AI model extracts key specifications and structures them into markdown, (3) the data is chunked and embedded into a vector database, (4) RAG retrieves relevant chunks to provide additional context for guidance. Evaluation used five generative AI models, RAGA metrics (faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision, context recall), task success rate benchmarks, and a course evaluation with 48 students.
mentioned_systems: SEMAR; GPT-4o; Claude 3.5 Haiku; Gemini 2.0 Flash; Mistral Small 24B; Llama 3.3 70B Instruct; RAGA
application_domain: IoT sensor setup and environmental monitoring (Smart Environmental Monitoring and Analysis in Real Time)
results_summary: The paper evaluated five generative AI models on extracting specifications from PDF datasheets of three unlearned sensors and assessed RAG-based guidance quality. GPT-4o achieved the highest answer relevancy (0.987) and best extraction accuracy, while Gemini 2.0 Flash delivered the most balanced overall RAGA score (0.76). The step-by-step guidance function achieved a task success rate above 80% across all models. A course evaluation with 48 students confirmed practical effectiveness, raising average test scores from 85.42 to 90.42 and yielding a usability score of 5.22 out of 7. No single model dominated all metrics, and context precision remained relatively low across all models, indicating retrieval relevance challenges.
limitations: No model achieved an overall good rating in extracting information from complex multi-column datasheet layouts; Context precision scores remain relatively low across all models, suggesting many retrieved chunks were not directly relevant; GPT-4o's faithfulness scores were lower than Gemini 2.0 Flash, meaning its answers were not always fully supported by retrieved evidence; The OUTTX110 sensor dataset exposed more gaps in both retrieval and grounding, as indicated by lower recall values across all models
research_gaps: Enhance the layout-aware algorithm for extracting PDF datasheets; Automate PDF datasheet retrieval using search agents; Add more accessibility to multilingual datasheets or users; Improve vector database accuracy by expanding abbreviation handling to enhance semantic similarity search and extraction robustness

research_focus: Enhancing clinical Named Entity Recognition (NER) by combining a fine-tuned BERT model for entity extraction with a Dictionary-Infused Retrieval-Augmented Generation (DiRAG) module for terminology normalization, addressing ambiguity and inconsistent standardization of medical terms in unstructured clinical notes.
method: A hybrid two-stage framework: (1) BERT-base fine-tuned on the MACCROBAT dataset for initial entity extraction, and (2) a DiRAG module that performs semantic retrieval from a UMLS-based vector database, lexical re-ranking combining semantic similarity with lexical overlap, and prompt-based generation using a large language model to normalize ambiguous or abbreviated medical entities.
mentioned_systems: BERT; BioBERT; ClinicalBERT; UMLS; Clinical ModernBERT; DiRAG
application_domain: Clinical NLP: named entity recognition and terminology normalization in unstructured medical/clinical notes (symptoms, medications, diagnoses)
results_summary: The fine-tuned BERT model achieved an F1 score of 0.708 on the MACCROBAT dataset, outperforming domain-specific baselines including BioBERT and ClinicalBERT. The DiRAG module further improved the interpretability and clinical relevance of extracted entities by selectively normalizing ambiguous or abbreviated terms using UMLS-based semantic retrieval and lexical re-ranking. Qualitative case studies demonstrated that the framework mitigates common issues such as abbreviation ambiguity and terminology inconsistency. The authors conclude that integrating semantic retrieval, lexical re-ranking, and prompt engineering produces reliable, context-aware, and explainable entity normalization suitable for real-world healthcare NLP deployment.
limitations: Manual evaluation of RAG-enhanced outputs was conducted on only 10 clinical notes, limiting the scope of qualitative insights; Evaluators were not trained medical professionals, raising the possibility of errors in assessing clinical appropriateness of substitutions; Evaluation is based on the MACCROBAT and AGBONNET corpora (300 notes from limited specialties), which may not fully establish generalizability
research_gaps: Larger-scale validation (e.g., 500+ notes) with scalable annotation infrastructure and domain-specific oversight is needed for stronger evidence of generalizability; Expert validation by trained medical professionals is needed for a more reliable measure of clinical relevance; Testing on broader and more diverse corpora such as MIMIC-III or multi-institution datasets is needed to fully establish generalizability; The full potential of RAG in clinical NER, particularly for resolving ambiguous abbreviations and normalizing terms, remains underexplored and warrants further investigation

research_focus: Optimizing Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) by exploiting sparsity and spatial locality in product quantization codebook usage, and integrating the accelerated ANNS pipeline into LLM sparse attention computation to reduce latency of the Q×K^T operation.
method: JUNO++ combines a sparsity-aware selective codebook construction algorithm (adaptive distance threshold filtering based on local density) with ray-tracing core (RT core) acceleration on modern GPUs. The RT core is used to identify nearby codebook entries via intersection tests, with time-based hit distance computation and Tensor-RT core pipelining. The system is further integrated into LLM inference to replace the standard Q×K^T computation in retrieval-based sparse attention.
indexing_methods: Product Quantization (PQ); Inverted File Index (IVF); HNSW; NSG
application_domain: LLM inference (sparse attention / retrieval attention), vector databases, recommendation systems, and Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
results_summary: The paper identifies redundant pairwise distance computation and codebook lookup as the key inefficiency in PQ-based ANNS, and exploits codebook-entry-level sparsity and spatial locality to design a selective codebook filtering algorithm mapped onto GPU ray-tracing cores. Evaluation on four datasets (1M–100M vectors) shows a 2.2× to 8.5× search throughput improvement over the FAISS baseline for low-precision search and 2.1× to 3.2× for high-precision search. When integrated into LLM sparse attention, JUNO++ achieves a 46% reduction in Q×K^T latency with almost identical accuracy in long-context scenarios (≥1M tokens). The authors note that gains are constrained by RT core performance and that the pipelining trick relies on a scheduling bubble that may be absent under aggressive fusion techniques like CUDA Graph or torch.compile().
limitations: Performance gains are constrained by the throughput of the RT cores on the GPU; The implementation is generally suitable only for long-context scenarios (typically exceeding 512k tokens); for shorter contexts the RT pipeline launch overhead dominates; The pipelining mechanism that hides RT pipeline launch overhead relies on a scheduling bubble between linear projection and attention, which may be absent on systems using CUDA Graph or aggressive fusion techniques such as torch.compile()
research_gaps: Cooperating JUNO++ with already proposed sparse softmax mechanisms to deliver higher end-to-end acceleration in LLM inference

research_focus: Development and empirical evaluation of a multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system that integrates textual, graphical, and tabular data using ReAct agent logic for multi-hop reasoning, addressing the limitation of existing RAG systems that handle only textual data.
method: The system combines semantic vector search with ReAct agent-based multi-hop planning, using separate ChromaDB collections for text, tables, and image captions with parallel searches (k=6), a 6:2:2 modality proportion for context allocation, and GPT-4 for generation. Evaluation was conducted on the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 with a test set of 50 queries (30 textual, 10 tabular, 10 graphical), measuring answer accuracy, recall, and response latency.
mentioned_systems: ChromaDB; text-embedding-ada-002; GPT-4; CLIP; Active RAG; REPLUG; Toolformer; ChatGPT; Google Gemini
application_domain: Multimodal document retrieval and RAG for information systems, empirically tested on medical/health domain data (WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 containing text, graphs, and tables)
results_summary: The proposed multimodal RAG system with ReAct agent logic was developed, deployed, and evaluated against a text-only RAG baseline using the WHO 2024 Tuberculosis Report as a multimodal corpus. The system achieved 92% answer accuracy, 89% answer recall, and 100% coverage across all data modalities, with an average response time of approximately 5 seconds. Empirically determined optimal parameters (k=6, classification threshold 0.35, up to three reasoning iterations) provided the best balance among completeness, speed, and efficiency. Comparative analysis confirmed that the multimodal agent-based approach substantially outperforms traditional text-only RAG solutions in accuracy and recall while maintaining acceptable latency.
limitations: The system represents images solely via their textual captions and therefore cannot answer questions about colours or shapes; Limiting the ReAct cycle to three reasoning hops sets a practical limit on recall, as additional iterations yield only marginal improvements while noticeably increasing latency; Response times scale linearly with prompt length; The linguistic nature of the embedding model means lemmatized captions provide less context than full paragraphs, slightly reducing discriminative power of their vectors
research_gaps: Integrating pixel-level embeddings (e.g., CLIP) as a separate collection to enable recognition of colours and shapes; Adopting active learning mechanisms for document selection (similar to Active RAG) to reduce context size without sacrificing recall; Adaptively increasing the number of reasoning iterations for more complex queries beyond the fixed three-hop limit

research_focus: The paper addresses the problem of tight coupling, interoperability challenges, and usability difficulties arising from proprietary APIs and vendor-specific query languages across diverse vector database management systems (VDBMSs). It proposes a model-driven software development (MDSD) solution centered on a domain-specific language (vecDSL) to provide a uniform, standardized approach to accessing and interacting with multiple vector databases.
method: The authors design and implement vecDSL, a prototype declarative domain-specific language, as the central component of an MDSD-based software system. The paper describes the abstract and concrete syntax of vecDSL, a code generator that transforms vecDSL models into executable code targeting different VDBMSs, and evaluates the language using syntactic metrics (token counts, nesting depth, keyword counts, Halstead Volume) compared against query languages of existing vector databases.
mentioned_systems: Milvus; OpenSearch; Apache Cassandra; Chroma; Weaviate; Qdrant; Pinecone; DeepLake; SvectorDB; Microsoft Azure AI Search; Elasticsearch; SQLAlchemy; TypeORM
application_domain: General vector database management and software engineering for uniform database access across multiple VDBMS vendors
results_summary: The paper proposes vecDSL within an MDSD framework to provide uniform access to diverse vector databases, eliminating the need for vendor-specific code. Syntactic evaluation shows vecDSL achieves 80 lines of code, 301 tokens, 49 keywords, zero nesting depth, and a Halstead Volume of 1681.45, indicating lower syntactic complexity than SQL-inspired languages (Milvus, OpenSearch, Apache Cassandra), JSON-based interfaces (Chroma, Weaviate, Qdrant), and MMDBMS solutions (Microsoft Azure AI Search, Elasticsearch). The results confirm that vecDSL effectively abstracts vendor-specific APIs and reduces the learning curve, addressing the uniformity and usability research questions. However, the evaluation also reveals that the absence of nesting structures and function calls, combined with a relatively high keyword count, may limit expressiveness for advanced query scenarios. The authors conclude that vecDSL is effective for basic vector database interactions but requires enhancements to support more sophisticated use cases.
limitations: The number of keywords (49 total, 17 distinct) is notably high, suggesting the language's minimalism could be further improved; The absence of nesting structures (maximum nesting depth of 0) and lack of function calls may limit the language's expressiveness and flexibility for complex query scenarios; The limited number of operations (66 total, 10 distinct) may restrict expressiveness for advanced query formulations; The initial evaluation focused solely on syntactic metrics without a user-based study, undermining validity, reliability, and reproducibility; No quantitative performance benchmarks (translation overhead, script generation latency, end-to-end query throughput) were conducted to assess runtime costs
research_gaps: Reducing keyword usage by consolidating semantically similar terms or introducing contextual keyword behavior to minimize redundancy; Introducing controlled nesting and basic function support to enable modularization and greater expressiveness while preserving minimalism; Conducting a user-based study applying a structured framework such as FQAD to involve both academic researchers and industry developers; Establishing comprehensive performance benchmarks measuring script generation latency, scheduler overhead, and end-to-end query throughput against native APIs and other high-level query languages; Conducting empirical evaluation of integration modalities comparing embedding as a language-specific module versus exposure via a language-agnostic API; Integrating vecDSL into existing programming language libraries (Python, JavaScript, Go) as a built-in module, library, or parser to streamline developer workflows

research_focus: Addressing limited access to timely, localized agricultural information in Africa by introducing an AI chat assistant that integrates Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and vector database embeddings to support farmers and extension workers in crop management, disease identification, and food security.
method: Integration of LLMs with domain-specific agricultural data through RAG, use of vector database embeddings for semantic search across agricultural datasets, a deep-learning CNN model for crop disease identification, and AI agents for autonomous task execution such as crop health analysis and predictive modelling based on weather patterns.
application_domain: Agriculture and food security in Africa, specifically crop health analysis, pest and disease identification, weather-based advisory, and extension services for smallholder farmers
results_summary: The paper introduces Abikn Noma, an AI chat assistant that combines LLMs, RAG, and vector embeddings to deliver context-aware agricultural advice to farmers and extension workers in Africa. A deep-learning CNN component identifies crop diseases with 88.3% validation accuracy. The system is reported to have the potential to cut 35-40% yield losses through timely AI-driven interventions. The assistant reduces reliance on a limited pool of human experts and enables scalable, real-time advisory services. The authors conclude that the tool enhances access to agronomic information and supports food security, while noting the need for verified content and improved rural connectivity.
limitations: Limited internet connectivity and poor network infrastructure in rural areas restrict access to the digital tools; Over 30% of smallholder farmers cannot read or write, limiting text-based interaction; Critical need to ensure the AI system provides verified agronomic advice, climate-smart practices, and weather-related recommendations; The agricultural sector has been slow to adopt AI technologies compared to other fields
research_gaps: Need for standardized digital formats and APIs to make accurate, up-to-date agricultural content accessible to AI platforms; Need for sustainable processes for content review and updates to ensure long-term relevance and ownership of information; Need to add voice and speech functionalities to extend AI's reach to illiterate smallholder farmers; Need to invest in rural infrastructure that supports connectivity and digital access for agricultural practitioners

research_focus: Designing a scalable, accurate, and hybrid code search method that combines keyword-based filtering and embedding-based semantic retrieval enhanced with LLM-generated summaries and semantic tags, supporting parallel processing and metadata enrichment for large-scale code repositories.
method: A two-path parallel search method with post-processing: textual keyword search (Elasticsearch with BM25) and embedding-based semantic search (Qdrant with text-embedding-ada-002) are executed in parallel. Code blocks are preprocessed using GPT-4o to generate natural-language summaries and semantic tags. LLM-based post-processing is applied to the top-most relevant results for line-level code matching within retrieved snippets.
mentioned_systems: Qdrant; Elasticsearch; GPT-4o; text-embedding-ada-002; OpenAI GPT models
application_domain: Code search and retrieval in software engineering (C#/.NET codebases)
results_summary: The paper developed and implemented a hybrid code search pipeline combining parallel keyword-based and embedding-based search paths with GPT-4o post-processing, validated on a .NET codebase of 25 C# files using 10 developer-like queries. The hybrid approach significantly outperformed both a keyword-only (BM25/Elasticsearch) baseline and an embedding-only (Qdrant) baseline in Top-1 precision, Top-5 recall, and MRR, particularly for queries with complex or abstract semantics. Average response time was approximately 0.90–1.0 seconds including LLM post-processing, deemed acceptable for interactive developer use. The combination of parallel search paths and LLM-generated metadata enhanced both result quality and responsiveness, confirming the practical applicability of the framework for real-time developer workflows.
limitations: Reliance on external OpenAI GPT APIs constrained by token-based limits and subscription-dependent rate quotas, impacting scalability in high-throughput or real-time scenarios; Additional latency introduced by LLM-based post-processing for line-level code matching; In high-throughput scenarios, batch processing or queuing would be necessary to avoid exceeding request quotas; Evaluation conducted on a limited codebase of only 25 C# source files, restricting generalizability of results
research_gaps: Optimizing embedding selection strategies; Integrating automatic query rewriting; Scaling across polyglot code environments; Reducing dependency on API rate limits and improving runtime performance in large-scale deployments; Incorporating static code analysis techniques (e.g., AST matching or control flow analysis) to enrich search quality; Developing domain-adaptive summarization models; Expanding hybrid retrieval methods into other software engineering domains including automated documentation, test generation, and intelligent code navigation tools; Integrating the hybrid method into development environments for contextual, in-line code discovery and reuse during software maintenance or refactoring; Improving the system through active learning and user feedback

research_focus: Proposing RAGMed, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based medical AI assistant for answering patient FAQs, scheduling appointments, and summarizing clinical notes, with a central comparative evaluation of two embedding models (gte-large vs. all-MiniLM-L6-v2) on retrieval quality and response groundedness in a clinical setting.
method: A RAG pipeline combining a vector database (containing ~45,000 doctor observations) with the LLM llama3-8b-8192. Two embedding models (gte-large and all-MiniLM-L6-v2) are compared using cosine similarity for top-5 retrieval, with responses evaluated via the RAG-Triad framework (context relevance, answer relevance, groundedness) on 18 real-world medical queries across three tasks: medical QA, appointment scheduling, and clinical note summarization.
mentioned_systems: RAGMed; llama3-8b-8192; gte-large; all-MiniLM-L6-v2; MedDialog; MIMIC-III; BioASQ; PubMedQA; i2b2/n2c2; NegEx; ClinicalBERT; BioBERT; RAG-Triad
application_domain: Medical FAQ answering, appointment scheduling, and clinical note summarization in healthcare delivery
results_summary: The paper presents RAGMed, a RAG-based medical AI assistant, and comparatively evaluates two embedding models (gte-large and all-MiniLM-L6-v2) within a clinical RAG pipeline using the RAG-Triad framework on 18 real-world medical queries. gte-large, owing to its higher-dimensional embeddings, retrieved more informative context and produced more accurate, trustworthy, and factually grounded responses than all-MiniLM-L6-v2. The system also demonstrated functional capabilities in appointment scheduling and clinical note summarization. The findings underscore that embedding dimensionality directly affects grounding quality in safety-critical medical domains. The authors position this as among the first evaluations linking embedding dimensionality to RAG performance specifically in medical dialogue and workflow support.
limitations: Absence of real clinical conversation data; reliance on public datasets that may not reflect the complexity and nuance of authentic patient-provider communication; Rare conditions, multimorbidity, and institution-specific practice styles are typically underrepresented in public datasets; The question test set of 18 queries is not sufficient for formal validation and serves only as an illustrative demonstration; The system focuses only on retrieval-grounded positive evidence and does not handle negative findings (absence of symptoms, normal results, non-diagnostic statements); Regulatory restrictions (HIPAA, FERPA) and IRB approval barriers limit access to real-world patient-doctor dialogues; Data de-identification challenges: conversational data often contain subtle identifiers making full de-identification technically and legally complex; Limited sharing agreements: health systems are reluctant to release conversational datasets externally due to liability, reputational, and security concerns; Resource and cost constraints in negotiating data use agreements, maintaining secure storage, and meeting compliance standards; The prototype is not designed for diagnostic use or treatment recommendations without professional validation
research_gaps: Exploration of voice-based querying to support more natural interactions; Integration with Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems for seamless clinical workflows; Development of advanced privacy-preserving mechanisms to safeguard sensitive health data; Incorporation of clinical NLP methods for negation detection (e.g., NegEx or neural approaches) to handle negative findings in the RAG pipeline; Involvement of physicians in iterative validation and co-design; Expansion of evaluation to widely used biomedical benchmarks such as BioASQ, PubMedQA, i2b2/n2c2, and MIMIC; Incorporation of statistical rigor through confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and effect size reporting; Evaluation on larger and more diverse question sets, including patient-specific queries linked to synthetic or de-identified health records; Incorporation of domain expert validation to assess correctness, completeness, and safety at scale; Validation using de-identified real-world clinical dialogues obtained under IRB approval and HIPAA-compliant data-sharing agreements; Safeguards for privacy, dataset bias, and responsible deployment

research_focus: A detailed exploration of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and memory systems for HR and enterprise AI, covering system architectures, embedding models, vector databases, and applications in recruitment, workforce planning, learning and development, and employee support.
method: The paper provides a structured exploration of RAG+Memory system architectures (four-layer design), reviews vector database design considerations and popular libraries, discusses synthetic experimental evaluations, and critically assesses ethical and regulatory challenges in the HR domain.
mentioned_systems: FAISS; Milvus; Pinecone; Weaviate; BERT; RoBERTa; OpenAI; Cohere
application_domain: HR and enterprise AI, specifically recruitment, workforce planning, learning and development, and employee support
results_summary: The paper systematically explores a four-layer RAG+Memory architecture (data ingestion, embedding/indexing, retrieval/reranking, generation with grounding) tailored to HR workflows. It reviews vector database design trade-offs (recall, latency, memory usage) and the role of metadata-aware retrieval for skill, role, and geography filtering. Applications in resume parsing, skill extraction, and candidate-job matching are discussed, showing how semantic retrieval improves accuracy over keyword matching. The paper identifies key challenges including PII privacy, embedding bias, model inversion attacks, and prompt injection, and proposes mitigation strategies such as redaction, debiasing pipelines, and encryption. It concludes by outlining forward-looking directions including multi-agent collaboration, cross-lingual retrieval, and federated memory systems for responsible enterprise AI.
limitations: Privacy concerns arise from embedding personal identifiable information (PII); Embeddings may replicate biases in training data, leading to disparate outcomes in recruitment; Security risks include model inversion attacks where embeddings inadvertently reveal sensitive data; Prompt injection attacks where malicious inputs manipulate model behavior; Explainability challenges: HR professionals and candidates require clear rationales for AI-driven recommendations
research_gaps: Multi-agent collaboration for RAG and memory systems; Cross-lingual retrieval in enterprise AI; Federated memory systems

research_focus: Developing a domain-adapted retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline that integrates geological knowledge with large language models to support intelligent question answering in the metallogenic domain, using the Qin-Hang metallogenic belt in South China as a case study.
method: A bilingual QA corpus was constructed from 615 authoritative geological publications. The corpus was embedded into a semantic vector database using Sentence-BERT and FAISS. The ChatGLM3-6B language model was combined with the LangChain framework to implement the RAG pipeline. Performance was evaluated using BLEU, precision, recall, and F1 metrics against baseline LLMs (ChatGPT-4, Bing, Gemini).
mentioned_systems: ChatGLM3-6B; LangChain; FAISS; Sentence-BERT; ChatGPT-4; Bing; Gemini; GPT; BERT; Anthropic Claude; LLaMA; BloombergGPT; FinGPT; MedPaLM; HuatuoGPT; BenTsao; GeoGPT; SkyGPT; K2; GeoGalactica; SciBERT; GeoDeepDive; GeoAI; SeisBench; Neo4j; macrostrat
application_domain: Geological knowledge engineering and intelligent question answering for the Qin-Hang metallogenic belt, covering regional tectonics, ore-forming processes, structural evolution, and mineral resources.
results_summary: The RAG-enhanced ChatGLM3-6B model achieved an F1 score of 0.8689, significantly outperforming the base model without the knowledge base (0.7969) and other mainstream LLMs including ChatGPT-4 (0.8514), Bing (0.8298), and Gemini (0.8146). The system demonstrated superior generation accuracy and content coverage for complex questions on mineralization mechanisms, geological background, and ore distribution. The approach showed high domain adaptability and reproducibility, with all datasets and codes openly released. The study confirmed that integrating a specialized geological knowledge base with RAG effectively addresses the limitations of general-purpose LLMs in domain-specific knowledge retrieval and response generation.
limitations: The current Qin-Hang metallogenic belt knowledge base remains limited in scope and does not comprehensively cover all geological characteristics, mineralization processes, and regional evolution; Knowledge base construction mainly relies on publicly available data and literature, lacking expert-validated ontologies or structured domain knowledge; Automated evaluation metrics (BLEU, precision, recall, F1) may not fully capture the depth of professionalism and practical applicability required in specialized geological domains; The knowledge base is statically constructed, lacking mechanisms for automated updates from ongoing geological research; The system does not yet support multimodal inputs such as geological maps, stratigraphic sections, or remote sensing imagery; The lack of expert-validated ontologies limits the system's ability to handle deep reasoning tasks involving geological semantics and terminology
research_gaps: Expanding and refining the knowledge base to more comprehensively cover geological characteristics, mineralization processes, and regional evolution specific to the Qin-Hang belt; Incorporating domain expert involvement to further enhance the accuracy and relevance of the knowledge base; Incorporating additional evaluation methods such as human expert assessments for a more comprehensive evaluation of domain-specific performance; Developing an automatically updated knowledge base to keep pace with ongoing geological research; Incorporating multimodal data such as geological maps and remote sensing images to enrich the model's interpretive and generative capabilities; Integrating expert knowledge graphs into the RAG pipeline; Testing the system's adaptability to other metallogenic zones; Incorporating multimodal fusion between textual and visual modalities

research_focus: Introducing a novel vector similarity search approach (ArrowSpace) that incorporates spectral graph properties beyond traditional distance metrics (L2, cosine) to capture structural patterns in high-dimensional data, and presenting its taumode indexing method.
method: ArrowSpace is a Rust library that combines traditional semantic similarity with graph-based spectral properties. The taumode indexing blends Rayleigh quotient smoothness energy from graph Laplacians with edge-wise dispersion statistics to create bounded, comparable spectral scores (λτ), enabling similarity search that considers both semantic content and spectral characteristics.
indexing_methods: taumode; HNSW; L2 distance; cosine distance
application_domain: Scientific and structured data applications; demonstrated with a protein lookup example (bioinformatics) on high-dimensional vector datasets.
results_summary: The paper introduces ArrowSpace, a Rust library that adds a spectral dimension to vector similarity search by integrating graph Laplacian properties with traditional semantic similarity. The taumode indexing method is shown to be memory-efficient while maintaining practical query performance, with a range-based lookup time complexity of O(log(N) + M). In the proteins_lookup demonstration, starting from a collection of λ values with a standard deviation of 0.06, top-k nearest neighbours can be retrieved via a range query on an interval of λ ± 10⁻⁷. The authors report substantial potential for improvements in downstream operations such as matching, comparison, and search, and note that the approach provides a foundation for multi-vector search by indexing sub-vectors of embeddings.
limitations: The current work is a core library only; a full database solution based on spectral indexing is not yet provided and is deferred to a future paper.; Further improvements in algorithms and idioms are needed to make the approach feasible and efficient in modern cloud installations.

research_focus: Designing a crash-consistent HNSW index for vector databases on persistent memory, addressing the problem that the original HNSW is implemented on DRAM which is costly and vulnerable to crashes, leaving the index in an inconsistent state after a system failure.
method: The authors propose P-HNSW, a persistent HNSW implementation on persistent memory that introduces a lightweight logging and recovery mechanism based on two logs (NLOG and NLISTLOG) leveraging byte-addressability and persistence of persistent memory. They analyze failure scenarios and describe the recovery process, then conduct extensive experiments comparing P-HNSW against SSD-based crash consistency mechanisms.
indexing_methods: HNSW; LSH; DiskANN; Annoy; k-NN; ANNS
application_domain: Vector databases for storing and retrieving high-dimensional feature vectors extracted from diverse datasets, particularly in the context of Large Language Model (LLM) applications.
results_summary: The authors designed P-HNSW, a crash-consistent HNSW on persistent memory, using a two-log mechanism (NLOG and NLISTLOG) to guarantee consistency during insert operations and enable reliable recovery after crashes. They provided a detailed analysis of failure scenarios showing how the logging mechanism ensures crash consistency. Experimental results demonstrate that the overhead of the proposed logging mechanism is negligible. P-HNSW achieves superior performance compared with SSD-based recovery mechanisms, highlighting the potential of persistent memory for building reliable and efficient vector indexes.
limitations: The approach focuses on HNSW, and its applicability to other ANN indexes such as DiskANN or Annoy remains an open question.; The evaluation was conducted on x86-based platforms with emulated persistent memory, so the behavior of P-HNSW on other hardware environments such as ARM-based processors or eADR-enabled systems may differ.
research_gaps: Extending the crash consistency techniques to a broader range of ANN indexes beyond HNSW.; Evaluating P-HNSW on diverse persistent memory hardware platforms, including ARM-based processors and eADR-enabled systems.

research_focus: Automated resume-to-job matching using semantic similarity, specifically designing and evaluating a Siamese neural network architecture with SimCSE RoBERTa embeddings to rank candidates by relevance to a job description, with emphasis on top-rank precision (Precision@10).
method: A Siamese neural network architecture using SimCSE RoBERTa sentence-transformer embeddings trained with MSELoss on paired resume-vacancy examples. The authors experimentally compared multiple base models (BERT, RoBERTa, SimCSE RoBERTa) and loss functions (TripletMarginLoss, CosineEmbeddingLoss, MSELoss, InfoNCE), and evaluated the final system against TF-IDF + cosine similarity, BM25, and Sentence-BERT baselines on a labelled dataset of over 7,000 resume-vacancy pairs from HuggingFace.
application_domain: Natural language processing applied to HR/recruiting: semantic matching of candidate resumes to job vacancy descriptions for candidate ranking and selection.
results_summary: The authors built a Siamese architecture on top of SimCSE RoBERTa embeddings trained with MSELoss and evaluated it on a binary resume-vacancy classification task derived from a 7,000+ pair dataset. The model achieved 72% accuracy, 70% precision, 74% recall, 72% F1-score, and 75% Precision@10, significantly outperforming TF-IDF + cosine similarity and un-fine-tuned Sentence-BERT baselines across all metrics. Among the tested loss functions, MSELoss combined with SimCSE RoBERTa yielded the best validation accuracy (73%), while TripletMarginLoss and InfoNCE showed retraining and inferior results. The system provides sub-5-second response times, integrates with a vector database for similarity search, and includes a feedback-driven retraining loop for adaptive improvement. The authors note that while results are promising, the 72% accuracy is not yet sufficient for fully reliable real-world deployment without further data and bias-mitigation work.
limitations: Dataset imbalance: approximately 66% positive and 34% negative examples after merging three original classes into two; Limited size and variety of the training dataset (~6,000 pairs), complicating generalisation; High semantic variability in job descriptions and resumes (synonyms, stylistic differences) that is difficult to capture even with modern transformers; Achieved accuracy of 72% is not high enough to be considered reliable in a real-world recruiting environment; Risk of algorithmic bias: the model can implicitly reproduce social or historical inequalities inherent in the training data even without explicit demographic features; Full automation and continuous integration of user feedback into training pipelines remain unimplemented; initial retraining experiments were conducted offline only
research_gaps: Full automation and continuous integration of recruiter feedback into training pipelines for self-supervised adaptation; Equity auditing of the model's recommendations; Bias reduction techniques to mitigate implicit social or historical inequalities; Integration of human validation in the decision-making process; Broader commercial deployment and domain adaptation to other HR or industry contexts; Scaling to larger, more diverse training datasets to improve generalisation

research_focus: Development and evaluation of a local, on-premises Agentic RAG system that orchestrates multiple LLM agents and vector-based semantic search to perform intelligent analysis of GitHub code repositories, specifically adapted for computer science education and IT practice.
method: A four-stage multi-agent pipeline was built by orchestrating existing components (LangChain, Redis, SentenceTransformer, LLMs): (1) query reformulation by a dedicated LLM agent, (2) semantic retrieval using SentenceTransformer embeddings stored in Redis, (3) response generation by a second LLM, and (4) relevance scoring via a verification agent with retry logic. The system was evaluated against two baselines (keyword search and a non-agentic single-stage RAG pipeline) using MRR@10, Precision@5, human Likert-scale ratings, query latency, and a SUS usability questionnaire.
mentioned_systems: LangChain; Redis; SentenceTransformer; Streamlit; OpenRouter; GitHub Copilot; Tabnine; Sourcegraph Cody; GPT; Claude; LLaMA
application_domain: Code repository analysis and software engineering education (intelligent analysis of GitHub repositories for explaining code, supporting self-learning, and knowledge control in CS courses)
results_summary: The proposed Agentic RAG pipeline achieved an average MRR@10 of 0.72, a 33% relative improvement over keyword search (0.48) and non-agentic RAG (0.61), and Precision@5 for code retrieval improved to 0.76 from 0.54 and 0.67 respectively. Human evaluators (n=15) rated generated explanations at 4.3/5 for clarity and correctness versus 3.6/5 for the baseline. Average query latency in the local environment was 3.8 seconds, deemed acceptable for educational and small-team use. A SUS questionnaire yielded a score of 78/100, reflecting positive user perception of the Streamlit interface and minimal setup requirements. The system demonstrated that multi-agent orchestration with iterative relevance verification measurably improves retrieval quality and explanation usefulness over simpler baselines while operating fully on-premises.
limitations: High computational cost of running embeddings and LLMs locally; Potential hallucinations in generated explanations, particularly for complex or unfamiliar code; Inability of vector search to fully capture code syntax and control flow structures
research_gaps: Complementing the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) architecture selection with benchmark-driven evaluations for greater objectivity; Model personalisation for specific user or codebase contexts; Integration of a broader range of programming languages; Development of more complex agent-based scenarios

research_focus: Proposing a novel adaptive algorithm for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search that dynamically determines the number of clusters to probe in an inverted file (IVF) index based on online query complexity classification, aiming to improve search speed while maintaining high Recall.
method: The algorithm performs an initial trial search in a limited number of clusters to assess query complexity, then uses a lightweight classifier (trained on a single feature: the number of productive clusters) to dynamically determine the sufficient number of clusters (nprobes) for each query. The classifier is built using features derived from the IVF structure (number of effective clusters, variance of distances to retrieved neighbors, proximity to cluster centroids) and is designed to be integrated on top of existing IVF indexes in vector database systems.
indexing_methods: IVF; HNSW; LSH; PQ; KD-tree; R-tree; B+-tree; Cover-tree; NSW; VA-File; IMI; NSG; LPH
application_domain: General vector database search and approximate nearest neighbor retrieval, with references to recommendation systems, fraud detection, image processing, information retrieval, and traffic simulation as downstream application areas.
results_summary: The proposed adaptive IVF search algorithm dynamically calibrates the number of clusters to probe per query using a lightweight complexity classifier, achieving up to 28.93% increase in QPS and up to 22.7% reduction in average latency compared to the standard IVF algorithm while maintaining Recall@100 ≥ 0.99. The algorithm is deterministic and requires no structural modifications to the existing IVF index, only lightweight metadata augmentation. Experiments on datasets up to 1 billion vectors confirmed scalability, and the use of greedy agglomerative clustering showed improved Recall stability. The results demonstrate that statistically guided sampling enables near-optimal Recall with substantially fewer distance computations, challenging the assumption that higher Recall necessarily requires probing more clusters.
limitations: The classifier requires a training phase with exact nearest neighbor annotations for a representative query sample, introducing non-trivial overhead during index construction.; The current implementation assumes a single fixed Recall target (Recall@100 ≥ 0.99) rather than supporting variable targets.; Experiments focus on Euclidean distance and IVF-Flat, limiting demonstrated generality to other distance metrics or quantization schemes.
research_gaps: Investigating semi-supervised or online learning strategies that enable incremental refinement of the classifier during production use.; Extending the framework to support multi-objective optimization, e.g. balancing Recall against latency under dynamic SLAs in cloud-native vector databases.; Generalizing the early-termination principle to other quantization schemes (such as PQ+IVF) and indexing structures (such as HNSW) where similar early-stage diagnostic features can be extracted.

research_focus: Developing a comprehensive methodology for measuring and optimizing RAG systems by analyzing the combined impact of chunk size, vector embedding models, and LLM selection on overall system effectiveness, particularly in the context of long-form internal documents.
method: Experimental evaluation of 48 configuration variants (different chunk sizes, embedding models, and LLMs) on a large biographical dataset stored in Qdrant, using stratified random sampling of 300 questions per experiment and LLM-based evaluation of both vector DB retrieval accuracy and final response quality.
mentioned_systems: Qdrant; Pinecone; Weaviate; Milvus; bge-small-en-v1.5; bge-base-en-v1.5; bge-large-en-v1.5; Gemini-2.0-flash; Gemini-2.0-flash-lite; Mistral-saba-24b; Gemma2-9b-it
application_domain: Retrieval-augmented generation over long-form biographical text data, with broader applicability to internal company knowledge bases in business contexts
results_summary: The paper addressed the lack of a unified methodology for RAG optimization by conducting 48 experiments comparing different combinations of chunk sizes, embedding models, and LLMs on a biographical dataset. Results demonstrated that optimal parameter selection is a multidimensional trade-off between response quality, computational cost, and hardware constraints. LLM context window size was found to be a critical factor, as it determines the maximum number of retrievable chunks and thus affects response precision. research_focus: Automating candidate gene prioritization for sepsis research using large language models, addressing the limitations of naive LLM approaches (hallucination, lack of systematic validation) by combining LLM-based screening with retrieval-augmented generation and literature-grounded faithfulness evaluation.
method: A three-stage computational pipeline: (1) composite scoring of all genes using a naive LLM, (2) filtering through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using 6,346 curated sepsis publications with dual-model faithfulness checks, and (3) multi-dimensional optimization with Chain-of-Thought hybrid reasoning. Applied to 10,824 genes from the BloodGen3 repertoire, with benchmark validation against expert-curated databases.
mentioned_systems: GPT-4; GPT-4o; GPT-4T; Claude; PaLM; ProGENI; Monarch Initiative; GeneRAG; MIRAGE; AlzheimerRAG; DRAGON-AI; Genie; BloodGen3
application_domain: Sepsis research: therapeutic target identification and biomarker discovery from transcriptomic data
results_summary: The framework progressively filtered 10,824 genes down to 30 ultra-high confidence sepsis-relevant therapeutic candidates, achieving 94% filtering efficiency and strong enrichment for inflammatory pathways (TNF-α signaling, complement activation, interferon responses). Benchmark validation against expert-curated databases achieved 71.2% recall with systematic correlation between computational confidence and evidence quality, substantially exceeding recent LLM applications. The final candidate set balanced discovery (11 novel genes) with validation (19 known genes), maintaining biological coherence throughout. Dual-evaluator faithfulness assessment achieved 71.94% inter-evaluator agreement, and 74% agreement between GPT-4o and GPT-4T versions provided moderate confidence in cross-model robustness. The modular design enables adaptation to other diseases through knowledge base substitution.
limitations: Systematic blind spots in metabolic pathways (protein synthesis, urea cycle, cellular maintenance) likely reflecting literature emphasis on inflammatory over metabolic mechanisms; 30.5% RAG faithfulness pass rate may introduce bias toward well-studied genes; Selective loss of broader regulatory pathways (TGF-β signaling, EMT) in literature-validated sets suggests underrepresentation of resolution mechanisms; Sensitivity to model architecture differences, as shown by only 74% agreement between GPT-4o and GPT-4T versions; Potential circularity in scoring favoring well-published genes due to correlation with PubMed publication frequency; Substantial API costs and processing time may limit accessibility; Dependency on proprietary models creates sustainability concerns for long-term reproducibility as models evolve; Identified candidates represent prioritized hypotheses requiring extensive experimental validation rather than immediate therapeutic targets
research_gaps: Incorporating experimental data beyond literature analysis, including functional genomics and clinical outcomes data; Integration of tissue-specific and temporal expression patterns for context-relevant prioritization; Expanding beyond inflammatory mechanisms to include metabolic and repair pathways for more comprehensive target coverage; Continued validation against experimental outcomes and clinical data to establish real-world utility; Translating computational predictions into therapeutic advances through experimental validation

research_focus: Comparative statistical and performance analysis of three transformer-based embedding models (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2, all-distilroberta-v1) and their ensemble with PCA for enhanced vector search in a NoSQL database (MongoDB), evaluated on Wikipedia document retrieval using TREC questions.
method: 2,000 Wikipedia documents were converted into vectors using three transformer-based embedding models, ensembled together, and PCA was applied for dimensionality reduction before storing in MongoDB. Retrieval performance was evaluated using 996 TREC questions with metrics including Precision@10, Recall, MRR, F1 score, average execution time, and memory usage. Error analysis and statistical comparisons (histograms, scatter plots) were performed to assess semantic search quality.
indexing_methods: PCA; product quantisation; inverted file with flat vectors; graph-based ANN indexes; cosine similarity; Euclidean distance
application_domain: Text/document retrieval and semantic search over Wikipedia articles using TREC question-answer evaluation
results_summary: The ensemble of all-MiniLM-L6-v2, paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2, and all-distilroberta-v1 with PCA achieved the highest F1 score of 0.5094, outperforming all individual models in Precision@10 and Recall. While the ensemble increased memory usage to 924.79 MB and average query execution time to 0.1031 seconds, it significantly improved the relevant rate for raised queries. The all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2 models consumed less memory than all-distilroberta-v1 individually, but all-distilroberta-v1 failed to achieve a high F1 score despite lower query execution time. The authors concluded that the ensemble+PCA approach is suitable for large-scale dataset processing and real-time applications such as academic search platforms, digital libraries, and e-commerce.
limitations: The ensemble process abruptly increased memory usage to 924.79 MB, higher than any individual model; Average execution time for each query increased to 0.1031 seconds with the ensemble; all-MiniLM-L6-v2 produces narrow vector embedding values close to zero, failing to retrieve information effectively; all-distilroberta-v1 failed to retrieve information effectively compared to the other models despite lower query execution time; Higher dimensionality of vector data increases query execution time and creates complexity in finding similarity with large databases
research_gaps: Custom rule-based advanced filtering methods are needed to reduce complexity in MiniLM models; Transforming long texts into clauses can significantly improve similarity search for the paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2 model; The all-distilroberta-v1 model should be applied to complex queries rather than general queries; Limited explorations exist on MiniLM-based models for text-to-vector transformation and query retrieval using MongoDB; Computational efficiency and information retrieval from different queries have not been examined statistically in prior work
